articles.title: What would happen if an AI agent interfered with a Canadian election?
articles.summary: There are currently no provisions in Canada's electoral laws to address the prospect of AI agents acting without human direction trying to meddle in Canada's elections, says Canada's chief electoral…

image.caption: Chief Electoral Officer Stéphane Perrault, seen last year, testified before MPs on Thursday about AI and Canada's elections. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

There are currently no provisions in Canada's electoral laws to address the prospect of AI agents acting without human direction trying to meddle in Canada's elections, says Canada's chief electoral officer.
Chief electoral officer says there are no legal provisions to deal with AI acting alone

There are currently no provisions in Canada's electoral laws to address the prospect of artificial intelligence acting without human direction trying to meddle in Canada's elections, says Canada's chief electoral officer.
Speaking to CBC News after testifying before a parliamentary committee, Stéphane Perrault said he is not aware of any provision in the Elections Act that would cover such a scenario.
"The law is based on human accountability for their acts, civil or criminal," he said. "So, it always falls back to what are the people or the corporate entities behind that."

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly sophisticated, it raises questions of what would happen if an AI agent, which can independently decide to take specific actions, tried to influence a Canadian election but it couldn't be proved that there was a human in the loop or that a human gave it inappropriate direction.
"It's a really significant question," said Perrault. "What is the civil and criminal accountability of AI agents?"
Voters face 'challenge' of evolving AI use in elections, says chief electoral officer
Perrault's comments came after he faced similar questions during Thursday's meeting of the House of Commons committee on procedure and House affairs.
"We are seeing AI agents that are taking decisions that do not appear to be human driven. There's no person behind it," said Liberal MP Anita Vandenbeld.

"If an AI agent were to contravene the Election Act but it can't be shown that it was an individual — it was rather the AI agent making decisions based on their own…. This is in the future, I know, but how can you hold a computer to account for something?"
Perrault said Elections Canada's website is constantly under attack but there have not been any breaches.
"Your question is a very deep one," he said. "It goes well beyond electoral issues."
'A great hypothetical question'
Commissioner of Canada Elections Caroline Simard said it is something her office would have to examine more closely.
"It's a great hypothetical question," she said. "I would say right now we have new powers that can help us act on the current developments of AI but we would have to look into it further."

Vandenbeld also wanted to know what elections officials are doing to ensure that AI platforms can include credible information from their websites in their answer to questions from users. She said during the recent Quebec election, AI tools picked up information from one particular website because it was easier for them to read than more formal websites.
"It wasn't nefarious but it could have been," she said. "It could have been a foreign agent that would put this kind of information [online]."
Perrault said his office is working with AI platforms to ensure that Elections Canada's website can be picked up by the platforms.
"We are beginning to engage with AI platforms to ensure that our information is formatted, that it is presented in a manner that will be picked up by the platforms," he said.
"This is an emerging area for us but it is a very important one."

items: New foreign influence office won't prevent foreign interference, commissioner says
Foreign interference 'did occur' but didn't undermine integrity of vote, Hogue says
Loopholes could allow foreign money into elections, Perrault says

blocks.text: Conservative Rob Moore asked what Perrault and Simard are doing to counter any attempts to use AI to interfere in elections, pointing out with close votes, even a little bit of interference could have an impact on the results.
"Training, training, training," said Simard.

Perrault said attempts at foreign interference did take place during the 2025 election, such as attempts to target Conservative candidate Joe Tay, but it is difficult to ascertain impact and influence on elections.

"I'm not aware of any information or any evidence of impact on the election, so it's a negative statement in that regard," Perrault told the committee. "But it speaks at the same time to the importance of fighting these attempts. Whether or not they have impact, they do undermine trust in the electoral process."
Simard said her office is still investigating complaints received regarding the 2025 federal election but did not provide details of those investigations.

Large parts of southern and central Australia face elevated fire risk this summer, authorities say, while heatwaves and extreme temperatures are likely nationwide.

Most of Victoria, eastern Tasmania and large parts of South Australia, Western Australia, New South Wales and the Northern Territory face heightened bushfire risk – driven by high fuel loads, low soil moisture and forecast hot and dry conditions – according to the seasonal outlook from the Australian and New Zealand Council for Fire and Emergency Services (AFAC), released on Friday.

articles.title: 12 First Nations in B.C. buy stake in Coastal GasLink pipeline
articles.summary: A group of 12 First Nations in British Columbia are buying an indirect ownership stake in the Coastal GasLink Pipeline, backed by a $168-million loan guarantee from the federal Indigenous Loan…

image.caption: The Coastal GasLink pipeline transports natural gas to a processing and export terminal in Kitimat, B.C. (Coastal GasLink)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking

A group of 12 First Nations in British Columbia are buying an indirect ownership stake in the Coastal GasLink Pipeline, backed by a $168-million loan guarantee from the federal Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program.
Piece of ownership secured through $168M federal loan guarantee

A group of 12 First Nations in British Columbia is buying an indirect ownership stake in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, backed by a $168-million loan guarantee from the federal Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program.

On Thursday, CGL First Nations Limited Partnership (CGL FNLP) announced an agreement to purchase an 11 per cent economic interest in TC Holdco, a company owned by TC Energy that holds the company's 35 per cent limited partner stake in the pipeline.

This deal marks the second Indigenous equity partnership to buy into TC Energy's stake in Coastal GasLink this fall, following a $65-million federal loan guarantee announced in October for a separate, five-nation coalition.
Together, 17 First Nations along the route now hold an equity interest in the project.

"Our government is building a Canada where Indigenous Peoples are true partners, with the resources and opportunity to pursue their own ambitions and play a leading role in shaping the path forward. That is what meaningful reconciliation looks like in practice," said Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty in a statement.

Coastal GasLink is a 670-kilometre pipeline that carries natural gas from near Dawson Creek in northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada export facility in Kitimat. It is owned by Coastal GasLink Pipeline Limited Partnership, with TC Energy as the operator.
It is the only direct path to the West Coast for natural gas to be liquefied and shipped to Asian markets.

The terminal served by the pipeline, LNG Canada, is planning a major Phase 2 expansion, doubling its capacity from 14 to 28 million tonnes a year, putting it on the trajectory to become one of the largest LNG facilities in the world.
The federal Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program provides up to $10 billion in loan guarantees to reduce borrowing costs so Indigenous communities can buy equity stakes in major projects.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: Catholic maritime ministry plans expanded port visit for seafarers and fishers support
articles.summary: A ministry that caters to the concerns of seafarers, fishers, and their families has announced plans to expand its pastoral visits to more local and international ports, CBCP News reported.

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 5:28am
A ministry that caters to the concerns of seafarers, fishers, and their families has announced plans to expand its pastoral visits to more local and international ports, CBCP News reported.

Fr. Jose Conrado Estafia, national director of Stella Maris Philippines, said maritime ministry of the Catholic Church aims to reach at least 38 ports and that this would be part of an agreement with the Bureau of Customs.
In an interview over Radyo Veritas, Estafia said most of the targeted ports are international to allow the Church to reach more Filipino maritime workers.
He also said there are plans to "strengthen support for migrant and local fishers, as well as families facing challenges linked to overseas employment."
“We will be with them, walk with them, and journey with them,” he said.
The report also said that the national Stella Maris also aim to bring seafarers’ concerns to the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) and the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW).
"The organization plans to expand mental health programs by working with psychologists and other specialists, drawing on research into seafarers’ psychological challenges and coping strategies."
The organization launched its website, stellamaris.ph, at a conference held in Dauis, Bohol that is aimed at expanding its evangelization and outreach through digital platforms. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Ex-Conservative MP sues Liberal volunteer over alleged election campaign interference
articles.summary: A former Conservative MP is suing a Liberal volunteer, accusing the man of creating fake websites in a "malicious" and "calculated" plan to interfere with his re-election prospects during the 2025…

image.caption: Former Conservative MP Ryan Williams lost his re-election bid last year. He is now seeking damages for what he alleges was an attempt at interference by a Liberal campaign volunteer. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics

A former Conservative MP is suing a Liberal volunteer, accusing the man of creating fake websites in a "malicious" and "calculated" plan to interfere with his re-election prospects during the 2025 campaign.
Defendant denies allegations, says lawsuit based on 'speculation'

One-time Bay of Quinte MP Ryan Williams alleges Steven Solarz — who had ties to the Liberal campaign that year — defamed him when he set up websites to make it appear like the Conservative camp was behind "deceptive" tactics.
Williams, who was elected in 2021, lost to Liberal candidate Chris Malette by 3,700 votes.

According to documents filed as part of the lawsuit, Williams alleges Solarz set up multiple websites associated with Malette's campaign. At least one of them, chrismalette.ca, redirected visitors to Williams's official campaign website, said his statement of claim.
Williams's case alleges Solarz was trying to create confusion and wanted the Conservative side to "be blamed, criticized or publicly associated with deceptive campaign tactics."

After the election, the former MP got a court order to compel the domain registration company GoDaddy and the Canadian Internet Registration Authority to disclose who was behind the websites. Solarz's name was on the domain registries, the documents show.

items: Liberal Chris Malette flips Bay of Quinte

blocks.text: "[Solarz's] conduct was intentional, malicious, high-handed and calculated to cause harm to Williams and to interfere with his campaign and electoral prospects," his claim says.

"The defendant's conduct occurred during an active federal election campaign in which Williams's public reputation, credibility and trustworthiness were central to his candidacy and electoral prospects."
Williams is seeking $1.5 million in damages.
The lawsuit was filed earlier this year but has recently nabbed local attention. None of the allegations have been proven in court.
Solarz denies allegations
Solarz denies all the allegations and in his statement of defence argues Williams's claims are based on "speculation" and "inference."

His lawyers have asked a judge to dismiss the matter, suggesting Williams's case is a strategic lawsuit against public participation (SLAPP) intended to interfere with Solarz's rights including freedom of expression.

In a statement through his lawyer, Solarz said he only got involved with the Liberal Party in 2025, ran for the nomination in March of that year and volunteered on Malette's campaign during the final two weeks of the campaign. He said he has no personal relationship with Malette.
"I welcome the opportunity to address Mr. Williams's claims in court," he said.
"I recognize that this has been an unfortunate situation. However, because the matter is before the courts, I am unable to comment further at this time."
Malette's office said he "unequivocally condemns the alleged actions and reiterates that this kind of behaviour has no place in our democratic process."
His office said the MP would not comment further while the matter is before the court.
Williams told CBC News he also lodged a complaint with election authorities.
Poilievre accuses Liberals of 'dirty trick'
During a news conference in Belleville, Ont., on Thursday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said it appears the Liberals played a "terrible, dirty trick."
Poilievre says Liberals might have played 'dirty trick' on former Conservative MP's campaign
"I hope that they answer for what happened here and that there is justice," the leader said.
"It should never be allowed to happen in our democracy. We welcome competitive elections that are hard fought, but there should not be this kind of fraudulent activity."

articles.title: A Boston man won $1M US in the lottery. Days later, ICE arrested him
articles.summary: Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales won $1 million US on a scratch ticket, the Massachusetts State Lottery announced Saturday. Three days later, he was arrested by immigration officials who said "his…

image.caption: Ariel Velasquez-Morales is seen in a photo posted to social media by Massachusetts State Lottery on Nov. 21. (@MAStateLottery/X)

blocks.text: World

Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales won $1 million US on a scratch ticket, the Massachusetts State Lottery announced Saturday. Three days later, he was arrested by immigration officials who said "his luck ran out."
The ticket 'ultimately led to his arrest,' ICE said, without elaborating how
Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales held an oversized cheque for $1 million US and smiled in the photo posted Saturday by the Massachusetts State Lottery.

Local media described the Boston man as "all smiles," reporting that he planned to save and invest his winnings after matching 11 words on a $10 US scratch ticket. Lottery officials said it was the first puzzle he'd ever scratched.

A few days later, his photo was posted online again — but this time, by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which said it had arrested the "illegal alien from El Salvador" on Tuesday. Now, Velasquez-Morales will remain in ICE custody until he's removed from the U.S., the agency said in a news release.

The ticket "ultimately led to his arrest," ICE said, without elaborating how. CBC News has reached out to ICE and not yet heard back. Velasquez-Morales does not yet appear on ICE's Online Detainee Locator System, where members of the public can search for people held in the agency's custody.
“Looks like his luck ran out,” said ICE public affairs assistant director Micah Bock in the news release.

On Nov. 24, ICE Boston arrested Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales, an illegal alien from El Salvador, during operations in East Boston, Mass. Velasquez-Morales entered the United States illegally on May 15, 2013. He was ordered removed by an immigration judge on April 24, 2014. https://t.co/YieIbY7afF—EROBoston

"Welcome to the ERO [enforcement and removal operations] Boston lottery! Where illegal aliens and sanctuary politicians are out of luck, and the law-abiding citizens of New England are always the winners!" ICE Boston posted on X.
It's unclear if Velasquez-Morales has legal representation. CBC News has reached out to several Boston-area immigration lawyers and not yet heard back.
A woman identifying herself as Velasquez-Morales's sister-in-law wrote on Facebook Wednesday asking for respect and empathy for him, his wife and children.
"There is a family waiting for him," she wrote in Spanish.
Another woman identifying herself as Velasquez-Morales's older sister commented on the same post, writing her wishes that he would soon be back home with his family.
CBC News has reached out to both women for comment and not yet heard back.
A photo of Ariel Velasquez-Morales posted by ICE in a new release on Nov. 25, announcing that ICE Boston had arrested the man a day prior. (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)
Can you win the lottery if you're not a citizen?

Velasquez-Morales illegally entered the U.S. in 2013 through the Texas border, according to ICE. An immigration judge ordered him removed in 2014, the press release noted, but "he illegally remained in the country."

While ICE posted on social media that "the rights and privileges reserved for American citizens are for American citizens," state lotteries typically do not require citizenship or residency — if you meet the age requirement and are physically present in a participating jurisdiction when buying the ticket, you can play.

items: What happened at the Seattle airport? Outrage as ICE arrests man and daughter boarding flight
Kilmar Ábrego García, who faced U.S. deportation efforts and 'vindictive prosecution,' arrives in Spain

blocks.text: CBC News has reached out to the Massachusetts State Lottery and has not yet heard back. But its website help desk notes that anyone age 18 and up who is physically present in the state can buy lottery tickets at retail locations and win prizes. The Boston Globe reports that the lottery also doesn't require winners to have social security numbers, but that non-resident winners often face higher federal taxes on their winnings.

Some U.S. states allow lottery winners to remain anonymous no matter the amount, others depend on how much a person win, but many — including Massachusetts — do not let winners claim prizes anonymously.
"The Massachusetts State Lottery treats a winner’s name, town and prize as public information and releases them," explains the Massachusetts Legal Resources website.
'They're taking my dad:' Masked ICE agents arrest passengers at Seattle airport
"The lottery’s position, and the state’s, is that publicity is part of the game: It demonstrates that real people win, and it deters fraud in the claiming process."
Michael Baker, a Massachusetts attorney who works with lottery winners, told the Boston Globe that immigrants may not realize how much exposure winning the lottery can bring them.
"I’m sure people, when they play, they’re not expecting being at risk of being arrested," he told the media outlet.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. articles.title: Albania's youth are protesting in Flamingo Revolution, not leaving the country anymore
articles.summary: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search…

image.caption: Most of the "Flamingo Revolution" protests in Albania have been peaceful Image: Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.
For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.
It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.
'Flamingo revolution' has broad support

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.
Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

blocks.caption: Clashes with police erupted in mid-October like here in TiranaImage: Adnan Beci/AFP

blocks.text: Alternating between Socialist and Democratic Party

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."
Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."
It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."
The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.
Protesters call out corruption, face high cost of living

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.
Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

blocks.caption: Albanians continue to call for the prime minister's resignationImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: Albanians largely pro-EU

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.
What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.
This article was translated from German.
Why Albania's political crisis is deepening

articles.title: Gerard Depardieu to stand trial in France for rape and sexual assault
articles.summary: The Paris Court of Appeal upheld the order for the 77-year-old French actor to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in 2018.

image.caption: Last year, Depardieu (center) faced trial for allegedly sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021 [FILE: March 2025]Image: Aurelien Morissard/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: French actor Gerard Depardieu failed in his attempt to overturn an order for him to stand trial on rape charges.

On Thursday, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that Depardieu should face trial for the alleged rape and sexual assault that occurred on August 7, 2018. However, the court dismissed the allegations relating to a second incident that occurred six days later.

Depardieu still has the option of appealing to a higher court. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told the Associated Press that she disputes Thursday's ruling, though she did not specify whether she will challenge it in France's highest civil and criminal court.

This decision comes just two weeks after the 77-year-old Depardieu dropped his appeal against a sexual assault conviction in a separate case. He accepted an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issued a public apology.
What are the charges against Depardieu?

An actress, who was 22 years old at the time, accused Depardieu of raping and sexually assaulting her at his Paris apartment on August 7 and 13, 2018. Depardieu was 69 at the time of the alleged incident.
She reported the allegations to the police a few days later. Depardieu denies the allegations, claiming that the encounter was consensual.
Last year, a trial was ordered regarding the allegations. If the trial goes ahead, Depardieu could face up to 20 years in prison.
Carine Durrieu Diebolt, the victim's lawyer, said that the Thursday decision was a genuine relief and a victory for her client.

blocks.caption: In France, Gerard Depardieu has become a very controversial figure because of the many allegations and obscene remarks he has made  [FILE: March 2025]Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP

blocks.text: Accusations overshadow Depardieu's legacy
Depardieu was born in 1948 into a working-class family in Chateauroux, a city in central France. He overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors.

The film star was a dominant figure in French cinema for half a century, becoming a renowned cultural export. He earned an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
Accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction, however, have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

The international media has also been paying attention to Depardieu's off-screen antics. One of the most notable instances was when he accepted a Russian passport from President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau junta delays presidential vote for 2 years
articles.summary: The decision came exactly one year after the military took power on November 26, 2025. The junta said the conditions were insufficient to hold presidential elections for now.

image.caption: The military took control of Guinea-Bissau last year Image: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

blocks.text: The ruling junta in the West African nation of Guinea-Bissau announced Thursday that it is postponing elections by two years until November 26, 2028.
What do we know so far?

The decision came on the 1-year anniversary of the military takeover in Guinea-Bissau on November 26, 2025. The country is currently led by military general Horta Inta-a, who serves as transitional president.
Inta-a said in a statement that there was "an insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the election.

"It is essential to guarantee effective conditions for preparing and holding elections in accordance with the principles of legality, democratic participation, equal opportunity, transparency and electoral integrity," he said.

The military coup in Guinea-Bissau came three days after a general election last year, with the military deposing incumbent President Umaro Sissoco Embalo. Both Embalo and opposition candidate Fernando Dias da Costa claimed victory in the election, with the military arresting Embalo one day prior to the results being released.
Guinea-Bissau army names general as new leader
What's the political and human rights situation in Guinea-Bissau?
West African bloc ECOWAS has urged Guinea-Bissau to transition back to civilian rule.

Guinea-Bissau is a small tropical Portuguese-speaking nation on the West African coast which has seen multiple coups in its history. The country faces a high level of corruption and is also a key point for cocaine trafficking to Europe.
According to Washington DC-based think tank Freedom House, Guinea-Bissau is only "partly free" due to military interference in elections.

Reporters without Borders ranksGuinea-Bissau 100 out of 180 countries on its press freedom index, saying the "sharp deterioration of security for media professionals, combined with political and economic pressure, has severely tested the practice of journalism in recent years."

articles.title: N.L. apologizes, says it now accepts Innu history dates back more than 300 years
articles.summary: The Grand Chief of the Innu Nation says Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham has apologized following a months-long controversy over the Innu's history in Labrador.

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
The Grand Chief of the Innu Nation says Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham has apologized following a months-long controversy over the Innu's history in Labrador.
Letter from Premier Tony Wakeham follows months of controversy
Innu Grand Chief emotional after N.L. premier accepts Innu timeline

"Newfoundland and Labrador accepts the position that the history of the Innu in Labrador goes back to the time of immemorial, prior to the arrival of Europeans," Jodie Ashini said on a Facebook livestream Thursday.
Ashini was reading a letter written to her by Wakeham dated Thursday.

items: Innu Nation grand chief says N.L. premier has more work to do after meeting in St. John's
Months after delay and ‘long, hard, painful’ path, Innu history exhibit opens in Labrador

blocks.text: The controversy has been making headlines since June, and boiled over when it was revealed that, according to the Innu, the province's archaelogy office only considered the history of the Innu to go back 300 years — which Ashini has called "a theory."

The tension between Ashini and Wakeham boiled over in September, when Ashini walked out of a meeting with Wakeham and later committed that the Innu Nation would not vote to support the new Churchill River deal with Quebec unless the province changed its tune on the Innu's history.
The pair held a nearly three-hour meeting earlier this month. Wakeham had previously committed to an independent audit of Innu records held by the archaeology office.

“I regret the length of time the controversy around the 300-year issue has taken to resolve. I apologize for the problems which arose from the province's position," Wakeham's letter, shared with CBC News, said.
Why is the Innu Nation upset with the N.L. government?
Speaking with reporters late Thursday afternoon, Wakeham said he had an emotional conversation with Ashini on Wednesday.
"To be brutally honest, it was emotional for both of us," Wakeham said.
"It caused me a lot of grief … trying to get to the bottom and understand all of it. And yeah, it was a lot of grief, I think, especially for the Innu Nation."
Federal clarification was what N.L. needed to hear: Wakeham
Wakeham was hesitant to take a stance on the timeline in the months during the dispute, often saying he wanted to wait to get the facts before making a judgment.
On Thursday, Wakeham told reporters he got those facts in October.

As part of land claim negotiations between the Innu, the provincial government and the federal government — which have been ongoing since 1977 — Wakeham said the federal government clarified that Innu have history in Labrador since time immemorial.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says the federal government clarifying to the province that the Innu have been in Labrador since time immemorial was what he needed to be able to move forward in addressing the wrongs felt by the Innu Nation. (Terry Roberts/CBC)
Following that clarification, Wakeham said he felt comfortable to move forward.

"Clearly, I don't see as a province how Newfoundland and Labrador cannot be on the same side as the federal government in acknowledging the Innu. And I spoke to the Grand Chief about that," Wakeham said.
"[I] apologized for the length of time that it had taken and regret the grief that it had caused the Innu Nation.”
Ashini wiped away tears several times throughout the livestream, expressing thanks for the support from "every single Innu."
“I don’t know if I thought this news would ever come, honestly,” Ashini said.
“I’m proud to bring you this letter that our history will forever be recognized that we were here longer than 300 years … and they’re not going to erase our grandparents and they’re forever marked."
Wakeham said he hopes the province and the Innu Nation can continue to work toward reconciliation.
"It was important for me to try to mend that relationship. None of us want to be at odds, and I think for both myself and Minister [Lela] Evans, that was important."

Clarifications

articles.title: Net migration to UK falls to lowest level since 1997 excluding pandemic
articles.summary: Latest figures show difference between number of people arriving and leaving UK was ⁠77,000 in ​year ‌to ‌June

blocks.text: Net migration across the UK has fallen to its lowest level since 1997 with the exclusion of the years of the Covid pandemic.
Figures released by the Office for National Statistics and the Home Office show that the difference between people arriving and leaving the UK was ⁠77,000 in ⁠the ​year ‌to ‌June ‌2026.
The ONS figures cover the year ending June 2026, down from an estimated 171,000 in 2025 and a peak of 944,000 in 2023. Annual net migration to the UK in 1997 was 48,000.

UK net migration is also for the first time in the “tens of thousands” since that target was set but never fulfilled by David Cameron’s government in 2010. An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated, according to the data published on Thursday.

The 62% fall over the past 12 months – from 204,000 in the year ending June 2025 – results from lower immigration. Net migration has fallen more than 90% since the peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023.
Immigration fell by 17% over the year to June 2026, driven by fewer non-EU citizens being granted permission to work, study, bring family members to the UK or apply for asylum.

Keir Starmer’s policies last year made care workers and some mid-skilled jobs ineligible for work visas, suspended family reunion for refugees and toughened restrictions for universities sponsoring international students.
Emigration remained relatively high but fell by 4% (-28,000) compared with the year ending June 2025.

Most people leaving the UK to live in another country were non-citizens who previously migrated for work or study, including those who moved to the UK as part of the “Boriswave” from 2021 onwards when immigration was unusually high.

Reacting to the figures, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said Labour’s policies should be credited for the drop. It will be seen as a boost to Andy Burnham’s plans to keep hold of “red wall” seats in any future general election.

“The Conservatives lost control of our borders. Year upon year, they promised they would bring net migration down to the tens of thousands. Instead, they let it reach close to a million a year, overseeing four decades worth of migration in their last four years alone.

blocks.caption: The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the government had ‘restored control’. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Reuters

blocks.text: “This government has restored control. Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people,” she said.
Burnham said of the figures: “I think we are finally, as a country, getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see.”

Asked about the UK’s future relationship with the EU and whether freedom of movement should be up for discussion, he said the Channel crossings crisis “arose significantly in the post-Brexit years when we lost that ability to collaborate with our European partners, and we’ve had to work hard to catch up again … So, no, I don’t think you can say that Brexit did anything other than weaken control of immigration in this country.”
The drop has been driven by policies pushed through by Labour and Conservative governments.

Home Office visa data from January to June 2026 shows visa grants to international students fell by 38% (-39,200) and grants to skilled workers including those in the health and care sector and their dependants also dropped by 38% (-26,300) compared with the same period in 2025.
after newsletter promotion
The end of social care visas has caused numbers to fall from 108,000 at their peak to just 1,400 last year.

Migration remains a key political issue, with Labour’s 2024 manifesto promising to reduce net migration, and aiming to “smash the gangs” involved in irregular migration and bringing asylum seekers across the Channel in small boats.

Burnham’s arrival in No 10 has signalled a shift in the way the government views legal migration. Some Labour insiders say that policy is now being driven by economic demands rather than a fear of the rise of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, which has suffered a dip in the polls.

The Conservatives claimed their policies under Rishi Sunak’s administration were responsible for the drop, including restrictions on family members that could be brought over by care workers and changes stopping dependants moving to the UK with international students.

Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said: “The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.”
Ben Brindle, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said net migration could drop even further next year, and may have a “fiscal cost”.
“We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall.

“Falling net migration is not automatically a problem for the UK economy, especially in the long run. Falling asylum migration is expected to benefit public finances. On the other hand, the number of migrants on skilled work visas has fallen even more over the past year, and that is expected to have a fiscal cost,” he said.

Sunder Katwala, the director of the British Future thinktank, said the figures “will come as a surprise to most of the public” who still tended to believe that immigration was rising. “It must now be time for the political and media debate to catch up and start a new phase of the debate about what happens next,” he said.

Other data published by the Home Office showed the number of asylum seekers living in hotels was at the lowest level since records began in 2022, but there was a 9% rise of those in “dispersal” accommodation – privately managed houses, flats or rooms in properties of multiple occupancy. There has been a drop in the number of new asylum applicants and Channel crossings are down 39% year on year, with 23,983 people having arrived in the UK in small boats in 2026.

articles.title: Nottingham man jailed for 12 years for drugging and sexually assaulting partner
articles.summary:
‘Depraved’ predator attacked victim while she was under the influence of sleeping tablets he had given her

A man has been jailed for 12 years for drugging his long-term partner and sexually…
articles.byline: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent

blocks.text: A man has been jailed for 12 years for drugging his long-term partner and sexually assaulting her while she slept.

The man, who is in his 30s and from Nottingham, cannot be named in order to protect the identity of his victim. At a hearing in June, he admitted sexually assaulting the woman on multiple occasions while she was under the influence of sleeping pills.
He was sentenced at Nottingham crown court on Thursday for two counts of sexual assault, six counts of assault by penetration and one count of possession of a class B drug.
The man wept in the dock as Judge Watson told him his sex crimes were “depraved” and “playing out a disturbing fantasy”.
“For a number of months you abused the trust inherent in any relationship,” the judge said. “You made excuses and shrugged off her concerns. She built up trust in you slowly that you betrayed.”
The court was told the victim was “particularly vulnerable” because he had given her sleeping tablets and sometimes wine that he asked her to drink. This induced a deep state of sleep.
The judge said the man would be subject to a sexual harm prevention and restraining order for the foreseeable future because he presented a “danger to future partners”.

Isabel Wilson of the Crown Prosecution Service East Midlands said: “This man sought to gain power over a woman who should have been at her safest with him, treating her as an object for his own sexual gratification.
“These were deeply predatory offences that involved a shocking abuse of trust, and the devastating impact of that betrayal cannot be overstated.
“I hope this conviction provides some sense of justice for the victim and demonstrates that those who commit such appalling offences will be brought before the courts and held accountable.”
The offending came to light after the man told a woman that he had been having sex with a woman while she was unconscious.
He shared images and videos of the abuse with the woman, including sexual touching and penetration, which prompted her to report him to the police.
Detectives then discovered that the woman in the photographs and videos was the man’s long-term partner.
after newsletter promotion
The victim also found a conversation between the man and another woman, in which he had shared an intimate video of her without permission.
The man had also posted sexual images and videos of his partner online without her consent, the court was told.
The case comes just a week after four men were convicted at Winchester crown court for sexual offences against Joanne Young.
She was drugged and abused by her former husband, Philip Young, who allowed other men to assault her in the family home.
He has admitted 48 sexual offences against her, while a fifth man pleaded guilty to rape and assault.
All six men are to be sentenced next month.

articles.title: Iranian journalist, Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian arrested in Tehran
articles.summary: Rights groups are calling for the release of freelance journalist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian after Iranian authorities arrested him at his Tehran home on Wednesday, a day after…

image.caption: The Committee to Protect Journalists called on Iranian authorities on Thursday to immediately release journalist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian after he was detained a day earlier by security agents and taken from his home in Tehran. (Jafar Panahi/Committee to Protect Journalists)

blocks.text: World

Rights groups are calling for the release of freelance journalist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian after Iranian authorities arrested him at his Tehran home on Wednesday, a day after he reported on an execution notice of two jailed protesters in Iran.
Mahmoudian reported on 2 jailed protesters at risk of execution day before arrest
Hosein Razzagh, a friend of Mahmoudian's and an Iranian activist based in Europe, told The Associated Press on Thursday that Mahmoudian was taken by security forces from his home.

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) said in a statement on Thursday that a source close to the journalist told the organization that Mahmoudian's home was searched and his electronic devices were confiscated before he was detained. The source spoke to CPJ on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, it said.

A message posted on Mahmoudian's Telegram channel later on Thursday said he had been charged with anti-government "propaganda against the regime" and "spreading false information." His detention was also reported on Wednesday by reformist news outlet Emtedad.

A day before his arrest, Mahmoudian published an execution notice on his channel that two protesters jailed after the 2022 nationwide "Woman, Life, Freedom" protests were at risk of execution within 24 hours.
Mahmoudian posted later that day that according to a lawyer and family, the sentences had not been carried out.
Iran officials behind deadly Amini protest crackdown named

The 2022 protests were sparked by the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini after she was arrested by Iran's morality police over allegedly not wearing her headscarf correctly. Amnesty International said in a September report that authorities committed crimes against humanity in the monthslong crackdown on the protests that left hundreds of people dead and thousands detained.

Mahmoudian, who co-wrote the 2025 Iranian film It Was Just an Accident, which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes, has campaigned openly on behalf of jailed protesters and those at risk of execution in Iran, Razzagh said, adding that Iranian authorities "are extremely sensitive about execution cases."
There has been no official statement or public comment from Iranian authorities on his arrest.
The Oslo-based Iran Human Rights group has said at least 15 protesters have been executed in connection with the protests over Amini, with two of the executions being carried out in 2026.
Mahmoudian subjected to severe torture

During a brief telephone call with his family on Thursday, Mahmoudian said he had been transferred to Greater Tehran Prison, just outside of Iran's capital. He said that security forces had severely beaten him during his arrest, leaving visible injuries, the source told CPJ.
Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said Mahmoudian was also reportedly subjected to severe torture in detention, to the point of losing consciousness, according to confirmed reports it received.

"Journalism saves lives, and Mehdi Mahmoudian’s courage deserves to be celebrated. Instead, the journalist has been arrested, imprisoned and reportedly tortured by the very authorities he exposed," said Jonathan Dagher, head of RSF Middle East, in a statement on Thursday.
"RSF stands in full solidarity with the renowned journalist and filmmaker and calls for his immediate release. Publishing information in the public interest must never be treated as a crime.”
In recent months, the Iranian regime has resumed its wave of arrests targeting media professionals, RSF said.

items: Oscar-nominated director Jafar Panahi says he will return to Iran despite looming arrest
Iranian singer subjected to 74 lashes for performing without her hijab
Amnesty report says Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in bloody 2022 protest crackdown

blocks.text: Razzagh told The Associated Press he last spoke with Mahmoudian by phone roughly between 2 to 3 a.m. on Wednesday about a death penalty case linked to the 2022 protests.
He said that Mahmoudian later didn't answer his phone, and that witnesses reported seeing more than a dozen armed agents raid his home.
The screenwriter and journalist has been repeatedly imprisoned for his work.
Mahmoudian was arrested earlier this year on Jan. 31 and subsequently released on Feb. 17, shortly before the Academy Awards, according to the CPJ.

His detention comes on the heels of Tehran's sentencing on Oct. 26 of his colleague and acclaimed director Jafar Panahi to five years and one month in prison. The Tehran court also ordered the confiscation of Panahi’s “movable and immovable assets."
Director Jafar Panahi poses on the red carpet at the Academy Awards in Hollywood on March 15. (Daniel Cole/Reuters)

Panahi, who directed and co-wrote It Was Just an Accident with Mahmoudian, returned to Iran in March after he had been previously convicted of “propaganda activities against the system.” Panahi has not been detained at this time, but his current whereabouts are unclear.

Panahi is among the most celebrated of contemporary Iranian directors and has continued making movies despite repeatedly being imprisoned, banned from travelling and put under house arrest by Iranian authorities over the past 20 years.

Mahmoudian and Panahi were among 17 Iranian activists, filmmakers and lawyers who signed a public statement issued on Jan. 28 condemning Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and the violent crackdown on protesters following mass anti-government protests in January.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Sara Jabakhanji is a Toronto-based senior writer assigned to cover news developments in the Middle East. She has worked in CBC bureaus in Ottawa, London and Toronto. You can reach her at sara.jabakhanji@cbc.ca.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Trump alleges ‘fake’ economic figures released before US midterms but doesn’t provide evidence
articles.summary:
In a Thanksgiving post, the US president seeks investigation after blue wave of Democrats unseat Republicans

Donald Trump has…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.

In a holiday message on social media tinged with bitterness, the US president wished a happy thanksgiving “to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%”.

While revisions to official economic figures are commonplace, Trump has tried time and again to challenge trust in economic data that does not support his claims that a historic boom is underway in the US.
The US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), an agency within the US Department of Commerce, calculates gross domestic product, or GDP, numbers.

“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Thursday. “This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error”.

Trump has repeatedly claimed since taking office in January 2025 that an economic “golden age” is taking hold on his watch. Many Americans have been grappling with a higher cost of living, however – exacerbated by the economic fallout of his war on Iran – and backed Democrats in the midterms.

Trump continued his acerbic well-wishing for “a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left” as well as “those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work”.

And he revisited another ongoing beef with the news media over his controversial focus on White House renovations and decorations. “I want to commiserate with those reporters and citizens who don’t understand filth, dirt, lack of maintenance, and corruption, and are upset with me because I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House.”
The sarcastic intervention continued with a message of thanks to “the murderers, drug dealers, and criminals of all shapes, sizes, and colors” whom he claimed are “mostly gone now”.

“Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from faraway lands,” he concluded. “We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!”

Democratic senator Chuck Schumer, vying to be majority leader in the chamber following his party’s victories in this month’s election took a more conventional approach, wishing “everyone in New York and across America a joyous and restful Thanksgiving holiday with your friends and family”.

Hakeem Jeffries, whom Democrats have nominated to be the first Black speaker in the House of Representatives, also played it straight. “Happy Thanksgiving to everyone in the community and throughout our great country! Grateful for the civil servants on the job who are working through the stormy weather to keep everyone safe,” he posted on X. “May God bless you all.”

articles.title: How much of the sharp fall in UK immigration is due to Labour’s policies?
articles.summary: Labour is jubilant it has got numbers down to levels the Tories could not but it was helped by factors beyond its control

blocks.text: David Cameron was the leader of the opposition when he made a comment on overall migration that was used to interrogate every Tory leader for the next 14 years.

Asked in January 2010 on the BBC by the interviewer Andrew Marr to address comments made by the archbishop of Canterbury calling for the population to remain under 70 million, Cameron said net immigration levels of 200,000 a year were “too much”.
“We would like to see net immigration in the tens of thousands rather than the hundreds of thousands,” he said.

It became a full-blown promise in Cameron’s Tory manifesto that year; and it was there again when he won the 2015 general election, alongside a promise to hold an EU referendum. And the promise was repeated by Theresa May in 2017 as she narrowly defeated the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn.
Both Tory leaders struggled with the actual net migration numbers, which fluctuated between 195,000 and 303,000.

Boris Johnson was pressed on whether he would revive Cameron’s pledge, and his 2019 manifesto said “overall numbers will come down”. Rishi Sunak, five years later, said he would like to see the figures get to tens of thousands but his manifesto promised that “numbers would fall every year”.
It has led to some crowing by Labour – and frustration from the Tories – that numbers have finally dipped below six figures under the current government.
Migration analysts said the Tories struggled throughout the 2010s because the UK was a full member of the EU and had no way of controlling inward EU migration.
EU citizens made up a majority of immigration and net migration in the run-up to the 2016 EU referendum. Since 2022, however, EU net migration has been negative.
As the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic, Johnson opened the doors to non-EU migration and to Ukrainians and people from Hong Kong.

Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said: “The previous government introduced some relatively liberal policies, including visa schemes for care workers, mid-skilled workers, Ukrainians and Hongkongers, and post-study work visas for international students.”
Several conditions that enabled Labour to achieve net migration of below 100,000 did not exist for most of the time that the Tories were in power, Sumption said.
First, the UK was part of the EU for most of the Tories’ time in office and so it had little control over inward EU migration.

Second, the Office for National Statistics still relied on an older methodology for estimating migration of British citizens under the Conservatives. The new method, introduced last year, has taken “tens of thousands off the net migration figure”, she said.
after newsletter promotion
Third, high migration under the previous government – and particularly under Johnson – has left a temporary legacy of high numbers of non-EU citizens leaving the UK under Labour.
“Non-EU emigration is around 130,000 higher than it was for most of the 2010s, and that is only possible because so many non-EU citizens arrived a few years ago,” she said.
The Tories throughout the 2010s were also under pressure from business and their own party to ensure that they could expand the economy and offer tax cuts, a former cabinet minister said.
“Migration was an issue then but not top of the agenda as it has been for the last few years,” they said.

The Tories claimed credit for the fall on Thursday, after introducing immigration restrictions in the last parliament. But Labour insisted it had been the one to “restore control” at the borders after net migration came close to 1 million under the Tories.
Sumption said the net migration figure could fall further but may also be expected to rise again.

“The lower figures we see today are partly a result of government policy but partly the result of methodological changes and an increase in emigration that is expected to be temporary. The numbers could still have further to fall but there is no reason to assume they will remain below 100,000 ffor ever, even if policy remains the same,” she said.
