articles.title: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos wins race to be next ECB president
articles.summary:
Former Bank of Spain governor chosen to succeed Christine Lagarde after winning support of EU’s biggest countries

Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos has been chosen as the next president of the…

blocks.text: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos has been chosen as the next president of the European Central Bank, to succeed Christine Lagarde, after winning support from the EU’s biggest countries.
The economist and monetary policymaker will become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB, defeating his rival candidate Klaas Knot, the former head of the Dutch central bank.

EU diplomats agreed two other appointments to the ECB’s executive board on Thursday: France’s Laurence Boone and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier. The trio of appointments was a package deal, after France and Germany converged on choosing Hernández de Cos, who is expected to keep the ECB on the same path.

Following the talks European Council president António Costa confirmed the three appointments, saying: “This will pave the way for the formal appointment of the new ECB leadership by the EUCO [European Council] in December.”
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, also confirmed: “A consensus emerged on the nominations to the European Central Bank.”

The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, who faces elections this weekend that he is predicted to lose, celebrated the victory of Hernández de Cos and the presence of Spaniards in other big EU roles, by hailing “a Spain that is leading in Europe as never before”.

Spain’s former deputy prime minister Teresa Ribera is one of the European Commission’s executive vice-presidents, with responsibility for a vast portfolio spanning the green transition and EU competition policy. The former Spanish economy minister Nadia Calviño leads the European Investment Bank.

Hernández de Cos, a former Bank of Spain governor, will become the fifth head of the eurozone’s central bank since it was founded in 1998. He is expected to take up his position after Lagarde stands down in February, during a time of political change and economic pressure in the 21-country eurozone.

Europe is entering a big election year, starting with Spain’s elections this weekend, with national votes to follow in France, Italy and (non-eurozone) Poland. European economies are under growing pressure from fierce Chinese competition, US tariff threats and soaring energy prices that are driving up inflation, as well as high debt in several member states.
One of his biggest challenges will be reining in surging prices: inflation in the eurozone hit 4% last month, up from 2.1% a year earlier.
Hernández de Cos, who is now serving as general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, is seen as supporting lower interest rates to boost growth.

Market analysts are closely watching what Hernández de Cos might say about France, where an embattled minority government is struggling to pass a budget. French debt is forecast to hit 122% of GDP next year, more than twice the limit allowed under EU fiscal rules.

Arne Petimezas, the director of research at AFS Group Amsterdam, said Hernández de Cos, who “leans dovish”, was the “continuity candidate”. He added: “Don’t expect de Cos to turn a blind eye to France and its fiscal predicaments. No carte blanche: bond buying will remain contingent on austerity and a path towards a lower debt ratio.”
after newsletter promotion

The ECB’s approach to the French debt crisis will come under intense political scrutiny, especially after calls from the French far-right presidential frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, “to ease the burden of interest rates”.

Hernández de Cos is seen as a central banker in the mould of Mario Draghi, the celebrated former ECB president and Italian prime minister, who is credited with stabilising the eurozone at a pivotal moment in the debt crisis. Matthew Ryan, at the financial services firm Ebury, said Hernández de Cos was “likely to place greater weight on growth, financial stability and fragmentation risk than Klaas Knot, the alternative candidate and a genuine hawk”.
“We do not expect his appointment to alter the near-term rate path. The president sets the agenda but is ultimately one voice on the governing council, and rarely overrides the consensus.”

The contest was set in motion less than a month ago when Lagarde, the ECB’s first female president, announced that she intended to leave her post nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront “the misrepresentation of the truth”.
Macron, who played a decisive role in appointing Lagarde, a former French finance minister, said EU leaders had welcomed her “decisive leadership during her term in office”.
Hernández de Cos’s appointment must still clear the European parliament and the ECB’s governing council, but these steps are seen as formalities.

articles.title: Marlboro maker Altria considering takeover bid for Imperial Brands
articles.summary: Shares in UK tobacco company jump by more than 14% on news US rival is looking into making offer

blocks.text: Imperial Brands could become the next UK company to fall to a foreign takeover after its US rival Altria announced a possible bid for the tobacco firm.
Altria, whose Philip Morris division makes Marlboro and Benson & Hedges cigarettes, told the City on Thursday that it was considering an offer. If made it was likely to be solely in cash, it said.
Altria also said it was in discussions with a third party about its possible acquisition of part of Imperial Brands’ business, suggesting the company could be broken up.
Under UK takeover rules, Altria has until 5pm on 24 December to either announce a firm intention to make an offer or walk away.
Imperial responded by saying it had not had any discussions “or received any approach or proposal from Altria or the third party referenced”.

It added: “The board is clear in its duty of aiming to maximise shareholder value and will consider any proposal, should one be made. Imperial Brands has strong confidence in its strategy and trading.”
The announcement from Altria came after Bloomberg reported that Japan Tobacco was ⁠evaluating a potential ​acquisition ⁠of Imperial.
Altria and Japan Tobacco are already partners in a joint venture, launched in 2022, to develop smoke-free ​products.

“A joint bid for Imperial from Altria (only present in ​North America) and Japan Tobacco would neatly swerve anti-trust objections to ​a possible takeover of Imperial Brands,” the RBC Capital Markets analyst James Edwardes Jones said in a note.
Shares in Imperial Brands jumped by more than 14% to the top of the FTSE 100 leaderboard, hitting their highest level since 2017. That lifted the company’s valuation to around £26bn.
Imperial makes a range of cigarettes including JPS, Davidoff, Gauloises and Lambert & Butler, Golden Virginia rolling tobacco, Rizla rolling papers and the Blu vaping brand.
after newsletter promotion
The company said last week that it was cutting as many as 4,600 jobs in a cost-saving drive as it used more AI and other technologies.
Imperial is one of the founder members of the FTSE 100, which was launched in January 1984.

Several other large UK companies have fallen to takeover offers this year, including the UK warehouse landlord Segro and the asset manager Schroders. The low-cost airline easyJet is in the process of being acquired.

The world’s largest catering company, Compass Group, also announced plans this week to move its main stock market listing to the US. Compass, which traces its origins to feeding British workers during the second world war, said it was making the switch because it had become a predominantly North American business.

articles.title: Trial of Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia begins after delay
articles.summary: Despite delays due to health issues, the trial of the Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia has begun. Prosecutors say the defendant used her military contacts to provide information on German…

image.caption: The espionage suspect, whose face is pixelated, was seen in a Ukraine conference in Berlin in December 2025Image: Ukraine presidency

blocks.text: The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman on charges of spying for Russia started Thursday.
The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.
Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses. Her lawyers caused further delay when they said she would not confirm her personal information.
Several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys said their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.
Espionage process with diplomatic fallout
The arrest of the 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman triggered a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.
The Russian ambassador was summoned regarding the incident, and Andrei Mayerov, the deputy military attache at the embassy, was expelled from Germany.
Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power.
Her full name has not been released due to German privacy laws. She was arrested on January 21 and put in pretrial detention.
The trial is expected to last until May 2027.
What is Ilona W. accused of?

She is accused of having contacts with current and former German Defense Ministry officials to provide information about defense industry locations, drone tests and planned drone deliveries to Ukraine.
She was also said to have been in contact with a man, her alleged handler, working for Russian intelligence at the Russian Embassy in Berlin since at least November 2023, prosecutors say.

On several occasions, she allegedly helped her contact at the embassy attend political events in Berlin under a false identity in order to establish contacts there. She is also suspected of having compiled background information on participants in high-level political events.
German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat
Berlin summoned the alleged handler, who was identified by Der Spiegel magazine as the embassy's deputy military attache, over the incident and expelled him from Germany.
Ilona W. led an advocacy group for years that called for international cooperation, focusing particularly on German, Russian, Ukrainian relations.
In addition to her advocacy work, she also ran a small marketing agency.
Both positions allowed her to be active in Berlin's political circles and provided her with connections within the military.
Russia rejects the allegations
The Russian ambassador to Berlin, Sergei Nechayev, denied the allegations this week.

"The Russian Embassy has no connection whatsoever to this woman, and even if she happened to cross paths with one of our representatives, perhaps at some reception, that means absolutely nothing," Nechayev told news agency AFP.
Why Berlin remains an espionage hot spot
He also said "he may have seen her himself at an event."
"But she is not a Russian citizen and, as far as we are aware, has no ties to Russia. She is a German and Ukrainian citizen, and, frankly, we do not associate with such individuals here," he said.

articles.title: Ontario will soon require licence, registration, insurance for e-bikes
articles.summary: Some e-bike drivers will soon have to get a driver’s licence, vehicle registration and insurance to ride on Ontario's roads, Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced Wednesday.

blocks.text: Toronto·New
Some e-bike drivers will soon have to get a driver’s licence, vehicle registration and insurance to ride on Ontario's roads, Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced Wednesday.
Province to require licence, registration, insurance for e-bikes that don't meet list of requirements
Ontario imposing new e-bike regulations from May 1, 2027
Come spring, some e-bike drivers will have to get a driver’s licence, vehicle registration and insurance to ride on Ontario's roads.
Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced Thursday that the province is tightening regulations on motorcycle- and motorscooter-style e-bikes, citing safety concerns.
"Simply putting pedals on a motorcycle doesn’t make it a bicycle," said Sarkaria at a news conference.
"If a vehicle looks and operates like a motorcycle, it needs to follow the rules for a motorcycle. It’s that simple."

items: Hidden cameras show some stores unlocking speed limits on e-bikes, selling e-scooters that go up to 120 km/h
Toronto police cracking down on e-bikes, e-scooters evading laws, regulations

blocks.text: Starting May 1, e-bikes in Ontario must have exposed bicycle-style frames, maximum motor-assisted speed of 32 km/h, and maximum power output of 500 watts.
The new regulations also divide e-bikes into two classes, each with maximum weight limits of 55 kilograms and 120 kilograms.
Vehicles that do not meet the requirements need to meet licensing, registration and insurance requirements to be on the roads.
People who violate the regulation will face fines of up to $2,500 and vehicle impoundment.

items: E-bike stores can modify speed control

blocks.text: Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow welcomed the regulations, saying it’s necessary for safety.
"We want to encourage people to not necessarily drive. Use other modes of transportation, but do it safely," said Chow at an unrelated news conference Thursday morning.
As of Nov. 22, police enforcement involving e-bikes has increased by 106 per cent this year compared to the same period last year, according to Toronto police Supt. Mandeep Mann.
There have been 909 reported collisions involving micromobility devices, including 364 involving e-bikes during the same period, Mann said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eleanor Yuneun Park is a journalist at CBC Toronto. She previously worked as a Content Editor at the Globe & Mail. She has an honours bachelor of arts in English and Religion from the University of Toronto. You can reach her at eleanor.yuneun.park@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Saudi pop music is thriving — but for the right reasons?
articles.summary: As part of Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's music scene has evolved hugely thanks to state funding and support. Local musicians and DJs are optimistic. But are they actually just helping prop up an…

image.caption: Although there are no pictures of state figureheads at big Saudi events, attendees say they know the state funds festivals and they suspect plainclothes security staff monitor the crowd Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: Today, rapper Asayel Bishi is one of Saudi Arabia's rising hip-hop stars, signed to the country's biggest record label for new music, MDLBEAST. But not so long ago, she was making international headlines for a totally different reason.

In 2020, after Bishi released a music video for a song, "Bint Mecca," or "girl from Mecca," featuring people dancing in a local cafe, Mecca's governor called for the arrest of Bishi's whole production team. He said the video violated the holy city's local customs and traditions. In the end, the situation was resolved with a discussion about filming permits.
And by early 2023, Bishi was signed to MDLBEAST and has since racked up hundreds of thousands of streams on music platforms like Spotify.

In the past, other Saudi rappers have ended up in prison for similar, alleged transgressions. The fact that Bishi's story went a different way is probably partially because the 31-year-old's career path is on a similar trajectory to the Saudi pop music industry as a whole.
Music part of Vision 2030

As part of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 plan, announced in 2016 and which aims to move the country away from economic dependence on oil, the country has poured billions into the local music industry.

The pace of development increased in 2019 after the country held its first major festival, Soundstorm, an annual event that now draws major international acts and over 400,000 guests. MDLBEAST was created then, primarily as the festival organizer. Since then, it has also become a record label, radio station, distributor, promoter and talent incubator.

blocks.caption: After decades of bans on concerts, the first officially sanctioned music gigs began to be held in 2017. Here, visitors arrive at the Soundstorm music festival in Banban in December 2025Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: A recent report for the Saudi Music Commission suggests the music sector could be worth $500 million (€455 million) by 2034. But it's difficult to figure out how well Saudi pop is really doing now because independent monitoring of the sector only began relatively recently.

Streaming platform Spotify reports that people listening to Saudi-made music inside Saudi Arabia increased by 195% between 2020 and 2024. However, the most-streamed artists inside the country are still international.
'Tied to the destiny of crown prince'
Although there was a mostly-hidden Saudi music scene before this recent boom, observers say the growth of the Saudi music sector is not organic.

It's all about building an industry from the top down, Amr Abdelrahim, a researcher at Sciences Po in Paris, reported in a 2024 study. "After 2016, young middle-class musicians and creative professionals, who had been careful to avoid drawing official attention to their countercultural activities suddenly became central to the ambitions of the state," he wrote.
The careers of young Saudi acts — like Bishi, for example — "became tied to the destiny of the crown prince," the researcher explained.

The Saudi royal family has long dispersed money from Saudi oil sales to their subjects, in order to ensure economic dependence and loyalty. But, Abdelrahim argued, "what is new about Saudi investments in culture under MBS is an unprecedented degree of centralization and the emergence of new clientelist networks around the country's de-facto ruler," using a common abbreviation for Crown Prince Mohammed.
Those involved "are inadvertently participating in the consolidation of the Saudi regime," he argued.

blocks.caption: Observers have noted the level of control around musical events in Saudi Arabia, with one researcher saying she was unable to find video evidence of bad behavior later, even though many visitors had filmed itImage: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: Observers say a lot of the new music businesses are vague about their ties to the state. But it's clear they couldn't work without the state's financial support and approval.

"Almost all major events are organized by the state or funded by closely linked entities," a spokesperson from Saudi-focused organization, ALQST for Human Rights, told DW. "This affects the type of music produced, as musicians have to be mindful of what is acceptable. This is not just about the music they produce, but also how they act and what they say to their fans."

ALQST believes Saudi musicians have even less artistic freedom under the new musical system than before, when they would have played or performed privately. They can lose their contracts and livelihoods, be prevented from performing or even arrested, ALQST's spokesperson said.
Hidden for two decades

"In the past, the music scene was not regulated," explained the guitarist and bassist for Saudi black metal band, Al-Namrood. But now that it is, the state can more closely monitor musicians who once stayed hidden and only played privately, the musician, who goes by the name of Mephisto, told DW.

Al-Namrood are one of the rare examples of a Saudi act that isn't working with state support. The group first formed in 2008 but have never played at home and have kept their identities secret for almost two decades.

"The exchange is clear: You want to perform, it has to be under our rules," Mephisto continued. "And I totally understand the perspective [of some musicians]. But typically the artist must refrain from any criticism of the religious or authoritarian. [The state] doesn't necessarily buy an artist's loyalty, it just creates incentives that make criticism increasingly costly."
For Al-Namrood, who have often condemned Saudi conservatism, religion and politics in their music, that's not an option. "We don't want anything to do with them," Mephisto said.

In her 2020 paper for the journal, Arabian Humanities, Nora Derbal, a professor at the University of Hamburg, said Saudi artists told her that if they got a call from authorities asking them to participate in a government project, it would be an offer they couldn't turn down.
The artists she spoke with were debating "their cooptation and loss of autonomy, and about the consequences for not joining in state projects," she wrote.

On the other hand, in various interviews, Saudi acts who have partaken in their country's pop music renaissance have also been positive: They don't have to hide anymore, they can play for larger audiences and they are paid. In an interview, one Saudi DJ described the first Soundstorm festival as like "Berlin after the fall of the wall" while others said they felt they were making history.

"So that's the interesting paradox," said Fannie Agerschou-Madsen, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Roskilde in Denmark, who's written several papers on the topic. "We have all these social liberalizations and challenges to conservative norms but at the same time that's not being followed by political liberalization."

blocks.caption: Before 2016, DJs only performed in private homes, compounds or beach resorts. One Saudi DJ described Soundstorm, seen here in 2022, as 'kind of our Woodstock'Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: Is the state co-opting local musicians?

But that doesn't mean that some room isn't being created for meaningful change, Agerschou-Madsen told DW. Locals told her they enjoyed the newfound freedom of going to a dance party although, she noted, the subversiveness seemed to be more directed at the social conservatism than Saudi authorities.

Young Saudis are well aware of the red lines and state control of the music scene and are continually negotiating boundaries, the researcher argued. In that way, "their everyday practices create space for political and social change, little by little, although perhaps not in what you'd consider a typically revolutionary way."
So is the Saudi state co-opting local musicians, including those who might have said something controversial before they ever get a chance to?
A DW enquiry to MDLBEAST was not answered. And the answer likely lies somewhere in the middle.

For some young Saudis, the new music scene has been about fun, self-expression, belonging and creativity, Agerschou-Madsen wrote in a new, as-yet-unpublished paper shared with DW. "Others, however, view it as a top-down project that commodifies fun while sidestepping deeper issues of political freedom and social equity."

articles.title: On farewell trip, Steinmeier calls for more investment in Africa
articles.summary: Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, Kenya: On his last trip to Africa, outgoing German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier called on companies at home to be bolder and seize opportunities in Africa.

image.caption: German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier (left) concluded his farewell tour to Africa with a visit to KenyaImage: Michael Kwena/DW

blocks.text: "My time as president is coming to an end, and that is why it was important to me to travel to Africa one more time — to the continent that is particularly close to my heart," said Frank-Walter Steinmeier during his final official trip to Africa. Over the course of 20 years, as president and before that as foreign minister, the veteran politician has made 30 trips to African countries.

"For me personally, things have come full circle today," the president added during his opening remarks at the German-African Business Summit in Ghana. He was alluding to the first German-African business summit in Berlin in 2015, which Steinmeier opened while he was still foreign minister in the administration of former Chancellor Angela Merkel.
This week, in addition to Ghana, he visited Cote d'Ivoire and Kenya with a business delegation from Germany.
Germany is competing — not just with China
A lot has happened since 2015, Steinmeier said. And yet: "We are still far from where we could be." Addressing Germany's business community, he said, "Be curious, take risks."
As the applause rang out after the speech, Jude Numfor, who works for the energy company REI in Cameroon, smiled. He too sees German companies as too risk-averse.
"When the Chinese come, they say 'let's do it,' and the Germans say 'let's prepare it'," he told DW.

blocks.caption: Steinmeier also visited Anno's One Fine Day arts center in Nairobi Image: Rosalia Romaniec/DW

blocks.text: Meanwhile, Africa's economy is growing rapidly. German-African foreign trade rose by 10.5% in 2025 to €63.4 billion ($69.4 billion). Africa's trade with the Asia-Pacific region is growing more slowly, but the absolute figures are also significantly higher.
This shows there is a great deal of potential in Africa's markets — especially in light of the emerging African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which encompasses most of the continent.

When it comes to direct investment, German companies are more hesitant than others — a trend observed not only by Numfor: China, Turkey and the Gulf states are willing to take on more risk and are pushing into these markets.

The Chinese, in particular, are offering large loans to build key rail lines and ports, and they are buying up mines and raw materials in Africa. But since they usually bring their own low-wage labor force with them, China's investments often create few local jobs.
Vocational training meant to open up new prospects

But such jobs would be the linchpin of Africa's future. In Kenya alone, 1 million young people enter the labor market each year; in Nigeria, the number is even higher, and some experts therefore anticipate even more irregular migration to Europe in the coming years.
Germany has said there is a need for action: It supports vocational training in Africa and, for several years now, has also been allowing skilled workers to emigrate to Germany from Africa.
Is China shaping Africa's mobility future?

During his trip, Steinmeier also visited educational institutions such as the vocational school for mechanics and industrial maintenance in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire. In Kenya, he spoke with President William Ruto about the implications of the 2024 bilateral migration and mobility partnership and more opportunities for language and vocational training.

There are now around 9,500 Kenyans working in Germany, and nearly 1,300 in vocational training. "We want to open up opportunities for young people and create regular, fair and orderly pathways for labor and skilled worker migration," Steinmeier said in Nairobi.
German SMEs also interested in Africa
Vocational training is said to be most effective where businesses and factories are being established.

"A very favorable window of opportunity for investment is currently opening up in Africa," said Fritz Audebert, CEO of ICUnet, a company that advises German firms on investment projects worldwide. "We've noticed a shift over the past two years or so, driven in part by geopolitical changes, the complicated situation in China, and most recently the war in Iran."

"More and more companies are beginning to understand this," Audebert added. "While there are reservations, we're seeing a similar sentiment to that regarding India." What's new is that small and medium-sized enterprises from Germany are also showing interest in Africa.

During the trip, Audebert was particularly impressed by Cote d'Ivoire, as he said, "because of the ministers' high level of expertise." The country is the world's largest cocoa exporter and possesses important raw materials. "You can work well with this potential," he said.
Opportunities for German automakers in Africa?
Members of the business delegation accompanying Steinmeier also agreed that the German automotive industry must focus more on the African market.
"The middle class is growing in cities, and with it, the demand for mobility," said Audebert.
Germany's FM stresses Europe's 'need' for skilled workers

Markus Thill, president of Bosch Africa, confirms there is a considerable market for simple, gas- and diesel-driven cars. "Based on the auto industry's experience, we know that households worldwide with an annual income of €10,000 or more can afford a new car," said Thill. This would mean that potentially 5-10 million new cars per year could be built and sold in Africa.
Instead, "we export millions of old used cars to Africa that would no longer be eligible for registration in Europe," he said.
Not just business: African nations as political partners

Even though the focus of the trip was on the economy, "we shouldn't limit our view to that," Steinmeier said at the end of his trip. Germany maintains a reliable political partnership with Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana and Kenya.
"These are three countries with which we cooperate closely on the international stage, and in that sense, visiting them now was the right and deliberate choice," he said.

When asked to take stock of his 30 trips to African countries undertaken during his political career, Steinmeier said: "There is not one Africa, but many, and there are also very different, uneven developments there." This fact, he concluded, needs to be "communicated even more effectively" in Germany.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte camp discloses 63-item evidence batch ahead of ICC trial
articles.summary: Duterte"s defense submitted 63 items, including a number of press articles, opinion columns, reports, lists of tables and graphics, photographs, ordinances, and legal and court documents.
articles.byline: JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN and ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III

blocks.text: Ahead of the International Criminal Court’s (ICC) trial of Rodrigo Duterte, his lawyers have disclosed a batch of evidence to the Office of the Prosecutor and the Common Legal Representatives of Victims (CLRV).

The latest filing, dated November 25 but released today, stated that Duterte’s defense submitted 63 items, including a number of press articles, opinion columns, reports, lists of tables and graphics, photographs, ordinances, and legal and court documents.
Legislation signed by Duterte into law
The filing is supported by an annex presenting document types and titles, including 17 laws signed by Duterte during his presidency.

items: R.A. 10932 — Anti-Hospital Deposit Law amendment
R.A. 11510 — Alternative Learning System Act
R.A. 11054 — Bangsamoro Organic Law
R.A. 10969 — Free Irrigation Service Act
R.A. 11310 — Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) Act
R.A. 11469 — Bayanihan to Heal as One Act
R.A. 11509 — Doktor Para sa Bayan Act
R.A. 11210 — 105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law
R.A. 11166 — Philippine HIV and AIDS Policy Act
R.A. 11036 — Mental Health Act
R.A. 11215 — National Integrated Cancer Control Act
R.A. 11346 — law increasing excise taxes on tobacco products
R.A. 11223 — Universal Health Care Act
R.A. 11148 — Kalusugan at Nutrisyon ng Mag-Nanay Act
R.A. 11037 — Masustansyang Pagkain para sa Batang Pilipino Act
R.A. 11463 — Malasakit Centers Act
R.A. 10931 — Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act

blocks.text: All except R.A. 10932 have been cited by lead counsel Peter Haynes in the defense’s pre-trial brief, released on November 25.

The other legislation mentioned in the annex—R.A. 11930 or the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children and Anti-Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Materials Act—lapsed into law on July 30, 2022, after Duterte’s term had ended.
The filing does not mention or explain how the defense intends to use each law at trial.

In the pre-trial brief, however, the defense cited Duterte’s initiatives in “free healthcare, education, and extensive drug rehabilitation programs,” which it said contradicted the prosecution’s allegation that he was responsible for a “widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population in the Philippines.”

The annex also lists two administrative orders, a 2018 board regulation and seven executive orders from Duterte’s presidency. These include measures on the government’s anti-illegal drug campaign, the nationwide Emergency 911 system, smoke-free public places, the 8888 Citizens’ Complaint Hotline, the whole-of-nation approach against communist insurgency, disaster rehabilitation, and access to medicines.
The annex does not state the specific evidentiary purpose for each issuance.
Davao ordinances, Duterte-era orders

The defense also disclosed eight Davao City ordinances covering women’s and children’s welfare, healthcare, public order, smoking, firecrackers, drug rehabilitation and emergency response. The annex lists the ordinances but does not state the specific evidentiary purpose for each. Several of these ordinances were signed during Rodrigo Duterte’s years as mayor of Davao City:

items: Ordinance No. 005004-97 — Women’s Development Code of Davao City
Ordinance No. 002491-94 — Davao City Children’s Welfare Code
Ordinance No. 000060-02 — Davao City firecracker ban
Ordinance No. 004-13 — Liquor Ban Ordinance of Davao City
Ordinance No. 000335-10 — ordinance creating the Women Health Care Clinic of Davao City
Ordinance No. 0548-16 — ordinance prescribing the functions of the Davao City Treatment and Rehabilitation Center for Drug Dependents

blocks.text: The annex also lists Ordinance No. 0367-12, or the New Comprehensive Anti-Smoking Ordinance of Davao City, enacted in 2012 when Duterte was vice mayor and serving as acting city mayor.

A more recent measure, Ordinance No. 0100-25, established the Computer-Aided Response and Emergency Dispatch (CARED) System. It was enacted in 2025, when Vice Mayor Sebastian Duterte was serving as acting city mayor.
Drug war, police killings, EJK reports
The disclosed material also includes reports and data more directly related to Duterte’s anti-drug campaign and alleged extrajudicial killings (EJK).

Among them are a media report titled “8.8M homes covered by TokHang when PNP led drug war,” a report on police use of deadly force in the Philippines, comparative data on police killings, and reports from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.
The defense also disclosed 4 media reports concerning the civilian-led EJK Truth Commission.
Other items include Philippine population and death-rate data and a report titled “The Cost of the Philippine Anti-Drug Campaign.”
The defense also disclosed a report by researcher Peter Kreuzer titled “A Patron-Strongman who delivers. Explaining enduring public support for President Duterte in the Philippines.”
In its introduction, Kreuzer wrote: “Duterte’s core message is one of discipline, iron-fisted assertion of order, and submission to the top strongman’s commands.”

The report, however, focused on explaining Duterte’s “enduring popularity”, asking why “such a national leader has managed to win and keep the hearts of the vast majority of Filipinos and Filipinas irrespective of socio-economic class or gender.”
Another Kreuzer report included in the disclosure is titled “Excessive use of deadly force by police in the Philippines before Duterte.” — BM, GMA News
Follow facebook.com/gmanewsonline for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: US army calls detonation of bomb chemicals in Iowa a success after fears of toxic plume
articles.summary:
The army blows up US stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used for explosives, to avoid uncontrollable explosion

The US army blew up the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical…

blocks.text: The US army blew up the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used to make explosives, saying the first checks show Wednesday’s controlled detonation in Iowa didn’t spread toxic dust to nearby homes and farms.

Earthen barriers were put up and foam and water were poured onto a pair of bunkers holding the 5 tons (4,500kg) of lead azide, and officials said those measures appear to have absorbed much of the blast.

The US Environmental Protection Agency air monitors were detecting no lead in the air around the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, and an alert sent to cellphones late Wednesday afternoon said it was safe to resume normal activities. Fema also issued an all clear around the plant, the US army reported.

Still, government agencies and independent researchers plan to do extensive environmental testing for lead – a heavy metal that’s especially dangerous to children and pregnant women – in the weeks ahead on water sources, farms, homes and playgrounds.
The army said the safest option had been detonating the stockpile right away because it was degrading and might explode uncontrollably at any time as the weather got colder.
Some experts cautioned that it’s too early to know whether communities are in the clear.
But Maj Gen Eric Shirley, who led the army operation, said the risk was “reduced as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible”.

Since the military announced and then delayed plans for the detonation over the past two weeks, residents and environmental groups have voiced concerns about potential health and environmental impacts and about a lack of information about what to expect.
The smoke after the blasts

An Associated Press reporter filmed the blasts from less than a mile away and upwind from the site. Following two loud booms around 9am local time, a pair of white plumes rolled high in the air before quickly dissipating.
The army attributed the smoke to the foam sprayed on the bunkers to tamp down any dust.
Bystanders who parked on the side of a road to watch came away unimpressed by the size of the explosion.
Burlington resident Tim Brandt said he wanted to feel the ground shake, but instead the detonation reminded him of the noisemakers that crack when thrown on the ground.
“It was nothing,” he told the AP. “It seemed like government put fear in a lot of people over nothing.”

The army scheduled the detonation for Wednesday because the winds were blowing to the south-west and away from populated areas including Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people along the Mississippi River.
The two controlled blasts destroyed all 68 barrels and didn’t set off any secondary explosions, Shirley said.
More lead test results needed
Donald Trump posted on social media that the army did a “great job”.
Acting secretary of the army Adam Telle along with the Republican governors of Iowa and Missouri also said it appeared to be a success and that the explosion was well contained.
However, the final results aren’t in yet, researchers said.

The EPA’s air quality data was promising, said Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters. Yet he stressed that samples need to be tested in a lab to determine if people face health risks.

“This should take days to weeks,” Whelton said. “But what we may see is different guidance issued to different communities based on how far they are from the detonation area and whether or not they were upwind or downwind.”

Colin Wellenkamp, the executive director of the Mississippi River Cities and Towns Initiative, said water treatment facilities along the Mississippi and Missouri rivers will be testing periodically to make sure that there are no detectable spikes.
Safety concerns and weather condition delays
Government officials had encouraged residents closest to the site and in range of the plume to evacuate and others to stay indoors.
Schools not already closed for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday canceled classes and many businesses closed. Some residents sealed their windows and doors as a precaution.
Doug Seyb, a livestock farmer from Donnellson, lives far enough away that he didn’t hear or feel the explosions. But he was still concerned about the accuracy of EPA air monitors.
“All of these cows are pregnant,” he said, “and we just cross our fingers that we don’t have deformed calves and stillborns.”
Army steps to quash the plume

A court ruling this week put the detonation, originally planned for last Friday, back on track. The army changed the date amid public backlash and to allow more time for safety measures and favorable wind.
The army set up “blast barriers”, with concrete and sand barriers two stories high. Ballistic gels, foams and water were added to absorb the dust.
Environmental groups who sued to halt the detonation said on Wednesday that legal action and public pressure forced the army to take more protective measures.
Had the blasts happened last week as planned, many safeguards along with clearer evacuation plans and expansive monitoring wouldn’t have been in place, they said.
“Iowa and neighboring states deserve a full accounting of why the situation was allowed to get to the point of crisis,” said Sarah Green, executive director of the Iowa Environmental Council.
Lead azide crystallizing

The stockpile was brought to Iowa from bases around the country in 2009, according to Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The lead azide was stored just in case the military needed to use it again.

During an inspection in March, staff at the ammunition plant found the chemicals had partially crystallized, making them sensitive to friction and cold temperatures and creating the risk of spontaneous detonation.

Some residents said the timing could have been better, given that it was the day before Thanksgiving, but they acknowledged it needed to be dealt with now. Others worried about the potential impact down the road.

“I don’t think lead danger goes away any time soon,” said Lucy Giehl, who lives nearby in West Burlington. “It seems someone might have thought about all of this a little sooner before it came to this.”

articles.title: UK bill to implement EU deal will allow ministers to enact closer ties in future
articles.summary:
Further deals can be enacted via same legislation, though it excludes rejoining single market, customs union or bloc as a whole

A bill to implement the UK-EU deal will grant significant…
articles.byline: Jessica Elgot, Lisa O’Carroll and Jennifer Rankin

blocks.text: A bill to implement the UK-EU deal will grant significant powers for ministers to enact even closer ties with Brussels, though it will stop short of Labour’s red lines.

The government put what it is calling the “cutting costs bill” before parliament on Thursday, beginning the legislation to put the deal into law after it was agreed with the EU last Friday – though the deal to ease access for food and drink exports will not come into force until 2028, with the emissions trading deal to follow that year.

The text of the deal published on Thursday confirms that although the UK will have input in designing future agriculture, food and emissions rules, it will not have a final vote. It will also contain a so-called Farage clause – a financial penalty if the UK or EU reneges on the deals over the next decade.

But UK negotiators said the deal showed there were significant wins in securing consultation with the EU at every stage of new rules being designed, rather than just at their final implementation, which had been the EU’s original position.
Hamish Falconer, the Cabinet Office minister and lead negotiator for the deal, wrote to opposition parties, including Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, on Thursday challenging them to support the bill.

“The status quo is not working. Brexit has done more harm than good,” the letter said. “A vote against this bill is a vote to maintain costly bureaucracy, to keep trade barriers in place and to hold back businesses looking to scale up into Europe.
“This isn’t about reopening the arguments of the past; it’s about fixing the problems in front of us and delivering the change the British people expect.”

The bill will enact the food and drink and emissions deals but retain powers for future deals to be struck – including one to create a common single market for energy which both sides have begun work on. The bill is a “framework bill” that leaves room for any future deals to be designated as “partnership treaties” and enacted via the same legislation – though it excludes rejoining the single market or customs union, or fully rejoining the EU.
The formal terms of a new youth mobility deal are still to be published, which will contain the final number of youth visas that will be offered to individual EU member states, totalling 100,000.
That deal will be tied to the food and drink deal, meaning that the closer trading ties will be cancelled if the UK reneges on the youth visas.

Introducing the bill, Falconer said the deal would reopen European markets to British products such as Lincolnshire sausages, burgers, seed potatoes, and shellfish, boosting agricultural exports by about 16% and adding up to £5.1bn a year to our economy by 2040, as well as frictionless trade between Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
The 80 page legal text of the food and drink agreement outlines the rules for a new common trading area, to which the “UK shall dynamically align and simultaneously apply”.

Under the deal, the UK will have a “consultative” role in EU legislation but “no voting rights” even in discussion on emergencies such as disease outbreaks. UK officials said that the UK would have a formal role in designing the rules and the ability to seek independent arbitration, but conceded it would not have final vote.
The deal also allows the EU to introduce temporary laws to “protect” the bloc in the event it cannot reach agreement with the UK on a particular issue to dynamically align.

Experts in the UK and member states will be “informally consulted”, which may not satisfy food industry bodies that have argued that British regulators should be involved in all the technical meetings before the drafting of EU laws.

EU sources have made clear that the adoption of the three main elements of last Friday’s reset will not take place until a separate agreement is reached on the level of tuition fees EU students will pay at UK universities. UK officials have firmly denied that is the case and insist the matters are separate.

An internal communication at the European council last Friday made it clear that the “adoption” or coming into force of the agreements were linked. “The Council agrees that adoption of the Council Decisions on signing of the ETS, SPS and YES agreements will not precede the conclusion of the negotiations on the supplementing Agreement providing for equal treatment on tuition fees.”

This creates a mechanism for a potential delay, mirroring the EU’s refusal to allow the UK associate membership of Horizon Europe until 2023, even through it had agreement in David Frost’s trade deal in 2020.

Burnham intimated in parliament on Wednesday that the two deals were not linked, citing the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen’s remarks on Friday that the fees agreement was “a separate piece of paper”.
But one senior EU diplomat said the agreements “will not materialise” without a deal on home rates on tuition fees within six months and there was “solidarity” among member states on this point.

A second senior EU diplomat said the UK’s handling of the tuition fees issue had been “toxic” and reminded them of the approach under previous governments led by Boris Johnson and Theresa May. “Nobody has charged British students [studying in the EU] any more since Brexit. This is why everybody is finding it a bit rich of them to insist on this.”

articles.title: Trump says he urged Putin to 'pull back' military aggression in Europe
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump claimed that he talked with Vladimir Putin about ceasing Russia's military aggression in Europe and expressed his belief in the possibility of a deal between Russia and…

image.caption: Donald Trump (left) and Vladimir Putin had a cordial meeting in China [FILE: November 19, 2026]Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Kremlin Pool/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said on Thurday that he had urged his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to cease "military aggression" in Europe during their talks in China.

"I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly," Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.

However, the US president did not specify which European territories he mentioned when communicating with Putin. This week, Poland — a NATO member — accused Russia of deliberately violating its airspace.

Trump added that he believes there is a "strong possibility" of such a deal between Russia and Ukraine. "Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH," he wrote in the post.
Is the Ukraine war ending? The meetings in Germany and China unpacked
Trump and Rutte call for 'peaceful resolution'
Trump's post on Truth Social came a day after he hosted NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Florida. They issued a joint statement afterward calling on Russia not to expand the war in Ukraine.

"We also talked about, at length, the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the War — and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the War, as rapidly as possible," the statement said.

Trump's comments represent a shift in tone after he cordially called Putin a friend during their meeting in China last week. Approaching Putin, smiling Trump said, "Who is he? He's my friend." Then he shook hands warmly with the Russian leader.
The echoes of the scene reverberated throughout Ukraine and other European nations, which are worried that Trump might side with Putin.
The US president had said he could end the war in Ukraine on the first day of his second term in office.
Europe's coalition trains for a role in postwar Ukraine
Russian refinery on fire after attack
Depite Trump's comments, the war shows no signs of ending, with both Russia and Ukraine continuing their mutual attacks.

A fire broke out on Thursday at the Slavyansk ECO oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region following a drone attack. The strike caused serious damage, according to a social media post by the company.
According to Reuters, two industry sources estimated that Ukrainian drone attacks have reduced the combined crude processing volumes of Russian oil refineries by 45% since late October.
At the same time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that Russia is preparing for a large-scale attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, logistics, and essential services.
Zelenskyy also said that crews are working to restore electricity in six Ukrainian regions after Russia launched ballistic missiles and 113 drones overnight.

articles.title: Lacson seeks return of P8.1B cut from DOTr budget for Davao, Cebu projects
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson on Thursday called for the restoration of the P8.1 billion slashed from the budget of the Department of Transportation (DOTr) that would support two foreign-assisted projects…

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 12:38am

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Thursday called for the restoration of the P8.1 billion slashed from the budget of the Department of Transportation (DOTr) that would support two foreign-assisted projects (FAPs) located in Davao City and Cebu province.
This was raised during the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P295.797 billion budget of the Department of Transportation (DOTr) and its attached agencies for fiscal year 2027.
In his interpellation, Lacson decried the P5.1 billion budget cut for the Davao Public Transport Modernization Program, as well as another P3 billion for the New Cebu International Container Port.
“Ito ‘yung mga growth-oriented investment na dapat nating i-prioritize instead of the usual…katakot-takot na ayudas,” he said.
(These are the growth-oriented investments that we should prioritize instead of the questionable financial aids.)

“These are, I think, priority, not only because it entails some payment of penalties and commitment fees, but because growth-oriented investment nga ito eh at saka commitment natin ito para hindi tayo makakuha ng loan (these are growth-oriented investments and this is our commitment so we don’t have to seek a loan),” he added.

Senator JV Ejercito, chairman of the Senate finance committee and budget sponsor for DOTr, noted the government already incurred P20 million in commitment fees and penalties due to delays from December 2023 up to June 2026.
Lacson warned that it may cost the government more if these projects do not resume by next year.
“Roughly, it’s about P3 million a year,” Ejercito answered.
Regardless, he acknowledged that these projects should be well funded as they will benefit the country’s economy.

“Anything for infrastructure. You know that’s one of my advocacies. Definitely, kapag meron tayong (if we get a) source, then I will also would want to restore instead of putting it in the smaller projects that have no impact,” Ejercito said.

The Senate finance panel chairman previously questioned the reported realignment of around P206 billion in the House of Representatives' version of the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.
Among the items he flagged was the P130-billion funding reduction for foreign-assisted projects.

He said the transportation sector also suffered a major cut of P40.4 billion, including P19.7 billion intended for the Metro Manila Subway Project and P15 billion for the North-South Commuter Railway. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Two Italians killed after Iranian strike in Kuwait
articles.summary: The pair were technicians for German company Rheinmetall, according to Italy's foreign ministry.

blocks.text: Two Italian nationals have died after an Iranian strike on a facility in Kuwait, Italy's foreign ministry has said.
The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, the ministry added.

Kuwait's defence ministry earlier said that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.
It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.
Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.
The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.
Meanwhile, Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement: "An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working."

The two Italian nationals were working at an air defence detection station and performing maintenance work on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa, citing Italy's foreign ministry.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.
"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

articles.title: Protests in Iraqi Kurdistan at plans for government in Baghdad to take over oil, border crossings
articles.summary: Thousands have gathered in the capital of northern Iraq's semiautonomous Kurdish region, waving flags and voicing opposition to plans for the federal government to take control of oil operations and…

image.caption: Image: Sabur Rashid/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters took to the streets of Irbil, also often written Erbil, in Iraqi Kurdistan early on Thursday in large numbers, waving massive flags of the semiautonomous region in northern Iraq.
They were responding to federal government plans announced earlier in the week for Baghdad to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had said the measures were part of a bid to stop oil smuggling when announcing the changes.
Rival Kurdish factions unite to protest plans

The plans marked an escalation in the long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities that have largely governed themselves since 1991, albeit with varying levels of recognition and authority.
Rival Kurdish parties joined forces for the large protests in the regional capital.

blocks.caption: Massive flags were set up to punctuate the demonstrationsImage: Mustafa Omar Ali/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protests were also reported to have spread to several other towns and cities beyond the capital.

Iraq's 2005 constitution, written following the US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein, formally recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But authorities in Erbil and Baghdad have remained in a tug of war over the control of land, oil and money ever since.

Tuesday's decision, which received backing from Iraq's Federal Supreme Court a day later, brings border crossing in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in four contested provinces — Kirkuk, Diyala, Salahuddin and Nineveh.
As US troops leave, Iraq faces new challenges

The Kurdish regional government's Cabinet said on Wednesday that the decision from Baghdad "violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan region," saying it represented "an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime."

Prime Minister al-Zaidi, who took office earlier this year with the backing of US President Donald Trump, also dismissed Kirkuk's operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflected Iraq's "independent national will."
Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by al-Zaidi's decisions and called them "completely unacceptable."

blocks.caption: The governments in Irbil and Baghdad have been jostling for influence for decadesImage: Mustafa Omar Ali/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Contested region even since 2005 reformation

Iraq's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the authority of the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) only covered the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the US-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein.
Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week's orders.

The 2005 constitution tried to solve the fate of some of the disputed territories in the lands between the borders to Syria and Iran that are home to a host of ethnicities and communities but with Kurds generally the majority group.

Article 140 called for reversing Saddam-era policies of expelling Kurds and moving Arabs in, and called for a census and a referendum on whether the disputed regions should join the Kurdistan region. Neither was held.

Kurdish forces then gained more of the disputed territory after Iraqi forces were forced out by the so-called "Islamic State," with Kurdish pershmerga for subsequently reclaiming some of the land with some international assistance.
The oil-rich region is highly important to both administrations, in a country that relies on oil revenues for the vast majority of its public sector budget.

Internal political tensions within Iraqi Kurdistan have further complicated the issue in recent months, with the Federal Supreme Court hearing an ongoing challenge against the current government's legitimacy after a party withdrew from the coalition cabinet. But rival Kurdish political factions seem to have found common ground on this issue at least.

blocks.caption: The demonstrations followed two days after the Baghdad government decree, and a day after it received backup from the Federal Supreme CourtImage: Mustafa Omar Ali/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

articles.title: KDgate for Montreal mayor continues with website mocking Kraft Dinner comments
articles.summary: Controversy in a box: Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada’s Kraft Dinner comments spark website, impromptu protest at city hall.

image.caption: Boxes of Kraft Dinner were already visible near city hall on Thursday morning. (Simon-Marc Charron/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal·Updated
Controversy in a box: Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada’s Kraft Dinner comments spark website, impromptu protest at city hall.
Soraya Martinez Ferrada acknowledged comment was awkward, but backlash continues
The controversy over her Kraft Dinner comments is sticking to Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.
The City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate – on Tuesday.
The budget is due to be adopted in mid-December.
But an ill-timed Kraft Dinner comparison over budget choices has been haunting the mayor, giving rise to a website created by a Montreal software developer presenting the city budget on KD boxes.
There is also a protest outside city hall later Thursday afternoon.
The landing page for the website, kdgate.ca, alludes to the mayor's comments. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)

Martinez Ferrada’s comments during an interview with French-language media outlet Quartre95, a personal finance site, following the budget rollout compared creating a municipal budget to decisions taken at home.
"We're going through every service to see what we can save. It's like when you make your personal budget: if you know you'll have less money one year, then, you have to make choices," she said.
"Sometimes, you'll have to eat a little more Kraft Dinner because you can't afford filet mignon."
The comments were walked back by Martinez Ferrada on Wednesday morning in an Instagram story where she described the comparison as “clumsy.”
"What I meant was that when we make choices, the city is the same as when we make personal choices," she said.
The website, kdgate.ca, includes a rundown of the city budget listed in a way that mirrors the nutritional facts on the back of a food item. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)
But not before it unleashed a torrent of backlash on social media, framing her remarks as out of touch with the reality of Montrealers dealing with higher cost-of-living.
On Thursday morning, a website, kdgate.ca, was published outlining a municipal budget in the form of nutritional information on the packaging of the popular comfort food.

items: Montreal mayor walks back 'clumsy' Kraft Dinner comment after major tax hike
Montreal's 'unprecedented' tax hike key to tackling 'infrastructure crisis,' mayor says

blocks.text: Niko Draca, the Montrealer behind the site, told CBC News about what prompted him to create the site.
"I saw a lot of outrage over the comment and I wanted to turn it into something positive and really get people looking at this data," Draca said.
"These documents are usually quite long and dry, so I figured a fun way to visualize could help, basically using the KD comment as a hook."
Meanwhile, a “Soraya Dinner” is planned for Thursday afternoon in front of Montreal’s city hall.
Organizers are inviting demonstrators to bring a pot, a portable stove and their own ingredients.
Montrealers 'already at Kraft Dinner,' says Centraide CEO on mayor's post-budget comments
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sidhartha Banerjee is an assignment editor based in Montreal. He previously worked at The Canadian Press and The Montreal Gazette. He can be reached at sidhartha.banerjee@cbc.ca.

articles.title: ICC Trial Chamber III sets conduct for Duterte trial proceedings
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - The International Criminal Court"s (ICC) Trial Chamber III has set the conduct of proceedings for its trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte, which will start on November…
articles.byline: Andy Peñafuerte III, Jay-vee Marasigan Pangan

blocks.text: Published November 27, 2026 12:10am

PRAGUE, Czech Republic – The International Criminal Court’s (ICC) Trial Chamber III has set the conduct of proceedings for its trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte, which will start on November 30.

Under the Chamber’s latest directions, the proceedings will begin with the reading of the charges of crimes against humanity to Duterte, as stated in the April 23 decision that confirmed those charges.
The Chamber will not read the specific incidents underlying the three counts to Duterte.
Following that, the Chamber will ask the former president if he understands the nature of the charges and give him the opportunity to enter a plea admitting or denying his guilt.
The opening statements will proceed with the following schedule:

items: Office of the Prosecution: 2 hours and 15 minutes
Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV): 1 hour and 30 minutes
Outline of the Defense’s case: 1 hour.

blocks.text: The first prosecution witness will testify immediately after the opening statements.
Hearing schedule
As confirmed by Trial Chamber III, daily hearings will have four one-hour blocks:

items: 10-11 a.m. (5-6 p.m. Manila)
3-4 p.m. (10-11 p.m. Manila)

blocks.text: The opening block of the proceedings begins on November 30 and continues until the court’s judicial recess on December 18.
The Chamber has also set the hearings on evidence for the first four months of 2027:

items: First evidentiary block: January 12-February 19
Second evidentiary block: March 1-24
Third evidentiary block: April 5-30

blocks.text: The court said it would set the schedule of evidentiary blocks “in due course” after April 30. It also announced that no hearings would be held on February 22-26 for courtroom maintenance, as well as on January 19 and February 11.
Witness schedule, Rule 68 requests, materials, and transcripts
Trial Chamber III directed parties in the Duterte proceedings to provide a schedule of forthcoming witnesses no later than four weeks before each evidentiary block hearing.
It also expects the parties to organize their witnesses’ appearance schedules so no gaps occur during testimony and to inform the Registry if their order changes.

The court also set deadlines for responses to Rule 68(3) witnesses applied for by the prosecution, and directed the parties to indicate the electronic registration numbers (ERN) of the materials they intend to use when questioning witnesses.
The parties are also instructed to agree on spelling and coordinate with the Registry to ensure accurate court records, and to inform the court if they object to the requested redactions.

The chamber’s direction comes as the prosecution, the CLRV, the defense, and the Registry prepare for the trial of Duterte, the first Filipino and Asian leader to face the International Criminal Court. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Georgia judge blocks own order to turn over US election ballot copies to state board
articles.summary:
Superior court judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe paused the order after county election officials filed a notice of appeal

A judge in Fulton county,

blocks.text: A judge in Fulton county, Georgia, has blocked her own order to turn over electronic copies of 2020 election ballots seized by the FBI in a raid to the Georgia state election board.
Superior court judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe paused the order after county election officials filed a notice of appeal.

The ballots are at the center of an ongoing dispute over the results of the 2020 election which some Republicans, led by Donald Trump, claimed had been rigged despite Joe Biden being certified after several recounts.
Republican state officials refused to overturn the result, despite a now-infamous phone call from Trump to pressure the Georgia secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, to “find 11,780 votes”.

Earlier this year, the FBI raided Fulton county’s elections office, seizing 2020 election ballots as part of an investigation into alleged “irregularities”. A federal judge later ruled that the government doesn’t have to return the election ballots after rejecting an argument by the county that the seizure was improper and unconstitutional.
The issue remains a political flashpoint, with Democrats questioning why the former director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, accompanied the FBI on the raid.

Virginia senator Mark Warner, a Democrat, said at a hearing in March he believed Gabbard’s involvement “potentially provide a pretext for the president’s unconstitutional efforts to seize control of the upcoming elections”.

Judge Ellerbe’s protective order said the state election board can use the records for its investigations but says the records cannot be disclosed to anyone other than people identified in the order, which includes the board members and staff, as well as experts they may consult.

articles.title: PAO proposes aligning compensation for unjustly detained with minimum wage
articles.summary: The Public Attorney"s Office (PAO) has recommended raising the compensation for victims of unjust imprisonment, detention, and violent crimes. It said the increase should be pegged to the minimum…

blocks.text: The Public Attorney’s Office (PAO) has recommended raising the compensation for victims of unjust imprisonment, detention, and violent crimes. It said the increase should be pegged to the minimum wage.

During a hearing on Thursday, the House Committee on Justice tackled House Bills 2337 and 2421, which seek to raise compensation for victims of unjust imprisonment, detention, and violent crimes and allocate funds for the payouts by amending Republic Act (RA) No. 7309.
The Board of Claims said compensation for victims of unjust imprisonment is currently set at P1,000 per month, capped at P60,000.
Lawyer Noliver Barrido of PAO said the current compensation falls far short of the daily minimum wage that an unjustly imprisoned individual could have earned had they not been detained.
“Ang PAO ay naniniwala na masyadong mababa po ang kompensasyon, ‘yung panukalang P5,000 o P10,000,” Barrido said.
(PAO believes that the proposed compensation of P5,000 or P10,000 is still too low.)

“Kung titingnan po natin kung ipe-pair po sa P5,000 kada buwan ang halaga po ng kompensasyon, ang ibig sabihin po sa isang araw o 24 hours na pagkakakulong ng isang tao ang ibabayad po ng estado sa kaniya ay P167,” he added.
(If we look at pairing the compensation at P5,000 per month, that means for one day or 24 hours of a person’s imprisonment, the state will only pay them P167.)
Even with a P10,000 monthly rate, PAO said this would translate to P333.33 per day, which remains well below the P755 daily minimum wage in the National Capital Region.
PAO said it also disagrees with setting a ceiling or maximum limit on the compensation.

“So ang isang manggagawa na papasok nang 8 hours at 20 days sa isang buwan ay kikita ng P15,000 mahigit. Mas mataas po ito as compared po sa compensation na ibibgay natin sa mga biktima ng maling pagpaparatang o bayolenteng krimen,” Barrido said.
(A worker who puts in eight hours a day for 20 days a month earns over P15,000. That is higher compared to the compensation we would be giving to victims of false accusations or violent crimes.)

“Hindi po categorical na sinabi sa aming position paper pero ginawa po naming batayan yung minimum wage rate po, at sana po ay i-peg po sa min wage rate ang bayad sa akusadong ng maling pinaratangan at dapat po siya mabayaran ang kada araw ng pagkakakulong at wala pong ceiling,” he added.

(It wasn’t categorically stated in our position paper, but we used the minimum wage rate as our basis, and we hope the payment to someone wrongly accused will be pegged to the minimum wage rate, paid for every day of imprisonment, and without a ceiling.)
The Commission on Human Rights and Gabriela Representative Sarah Elago both agreed with PAO’s suggestion.
Elago said even the P10,000 rate is far from a living wage, pointing out that the compensation should be enough to support a victim’s family.
Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville Luistro, the panel’s chairperson, said that while their proposals are understandable, budget limitations must also be acknowledged.

“We understand the point of PAO and the CHR that we have to consider the amount of minimum wage, as well as their leaning towards removing the cap. But let’s acknowledge also that budget limitations is real,” Luistro said.
During the hearing, the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR) said the law mandates it to allot 1% of its net income to the Victims Compensation Program.
While the agency agreed to the higher compensation, it opposed increasing the percentage share it contributes to the program.
PAGCOR said it has reservations about any corresponding hike in its statutory contribution, citing potential effects on the agency’s other mandated obligations.
Luistro said a catch-all provision will instead be introduced, granting the Board of Claims the prerogative to award compensation beyond the cap, provided it is justified.

“So perhaps in proposed catch-all provision, kung meron mga extraordinary cases na mare-receive ang Board of Claims, we can suggest in that catch-all provision to consider the minimum wage, to consider removing the cap for extraordinary claims of victims of violent crimes and unjust detention and accusation,” Luistro said.
She added that adjusting PAGCOR's 1% contribution would require a separate legislative measure.
The justice panel subsequently approved the bills amending Republic Act No. 7309.

Among the approved provisions is granting the Board of Claims the authority to award compensation exceeding the prescribed maximum limit in exceptional cases, based on the gravity of the injury and other relevant circumstances of the claimant.

“Taking into consideration the peculiar circumstances of each case, the gravity and extent of the injury or damage suffered, the duration and consequences of the unjust imprisonment or detention, the actual losses and expenses incurred and such relevant factors as may be necessary to ensure the compensation awarded is just, reasonable and commensurate with the harm suffered by the claimant,” read the catch-all provision presented by panel Vice Chairperson Rep. Bel Zamora.
The provision also directs the Board of Claims to state in writing the factual and legal basis whenever it awards compensation exceeding the prescribed maximum amount. —LDF, GMA News
