articles.title: FIFA says a cyberattack against it targeted a 'limited set of personal and business information'
articles.summary: World football's governing body says the cyberattack targeted personal and business information. They struck at a sensitive time for the under-fire organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.

image.caption: The cyberattack comes at the end of a rollercoaster year for FIFA and its president Gianni Infantino, who is now preparing his bid for reelection at a vote in March [FILE: June 10, 2026]Image: Alfredo Estrella/AFP

blocks.text: FIFA told news agencies on Thursday that it had been targeted by a person or group seeking access to its data.

"FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorized access to a limited set of personal and business information," a FIFA spokesperson told the Reuters news agency, issuing similar comments to other outlets.
Reuters cited a person "with direct knowledge of the matter" as saying that less than 0.1% of FIFA's total data had been compromised.
This person also said that no files from the controversial, abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project that looked to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors had been accessed.
What else did FIFA say about the cyberattack?
FIFA said that it was working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement, in the aftermath of the event.

It did not say when the attack took place, list the precise nature of the compromised data or specify how unauthorized access to FIFA data had been sought, amid reports of people having posed as FIFA officials rather than actually hacking the organization or otherwise compromising its cybersecurity systems.

"FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data," the Zurich-based organization said. "Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned."

Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot of what it said were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the cyberattack when responding to a post saying that more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been posted.
FIFA did not explicitly state whether it was talking about the same supposed incident.

The breach comes at a sensitive time for the organization. Still reeling from the scandalfollowing this summer's World Cup of its now-aborted plans to sell off World Cup commercial rights shares, it's now trying to secure another term for its embattled president, Gianni Infantino.

Infantino is the favorite for an election on March 18, when he is expected toface challenges from Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France. But until the turbulence of the last six months, it seemed most likely he would simply stand unopposed and extend his 11-year tenure without a fight.

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
articles.summary: A Paris appeals court rules Depardieu will go on trial for the alleged rape of Charlotte Arnould.

blocks.text: French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Mother of drug war victims set to observe Duterte's ICC proceedings in The Hague
articles.summary: The mother of two drug war victims is set to observe former President Rodrigo Duterte"s trial proceedings at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 10:37pm
The mother of two drug war victims is set to observe former President Rodrigo Duterte’s trial proceedings at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.
In a "24 Oras" report from Oscar Oida on Thursday, members of the group Rise Up supported Llore Pasco, who embarked on a flight to The Hague.

As an observer, Pasco represents the parents of slain drug war victims who could not afford to attend the hearings in The Netherlands. She lost two sons to the drug war on the same day in 2017: Juan Carlos Lozano and Crisanto Lozano.

“Sobrang importante po dahil yung iba po hanggang ngayon ay takot pa rin at sabi ko nga palagi dahil tayo ang naiwan, tayo yung buhay, sino pa ang magtatanggol sa kanila? Sino pa ang magboboses kundi tayong mga buhay,” Pasco said.
(It's very important because the others are still afraid and I always say that because we are the ones left, we are the living, who else will defend them? Who else will speak up but us, the living?)
Pasco brings with her the bag of one of her children. She prayed for strength as her fight for justice continues.
Rise Up covered the expense of Pasco’s trip to the Hague. Members made contributions so that she could make the trip, signifying that they were serious about justice.

“Yung aming paglalakbay, kasama ang pamilya ng biktima, ay talagang napakahaba, mahirap, masalimuot… Pero nang makita namin ang determinasyon ng mga pamilya, lalo na yung mga nanay, yung mga nawalan ng anak, yung mga nawalan ng asawa, yung kanilang determinasyon. Sabi nga ng isang nanay, ‘alam ko dapat may hustisya pero di ko alam kung paano’,” Rise Up Coordinator Rubylin Litaw said.

(Our journey, together with the family of the victims, is so long, difficult, complicated... But when we saw the determination of the families, especially the mothers who lost their children, who lost their husbands, their determination. One of the mothers said ‘I know that there should be justice, but I do not know how to attain it.) — Jean Mangaluz/BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
articles.summary: Rebecca Taylor had been imprisoned in New Mexico for multiple theft and burglary charges.

blocks.text: A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.
The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.
She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.
Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.
The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.

The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.
"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.
All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.
However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.
The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon used his service weapon to murder two men. Did NSW police recruiters miss any red flags?
articles.summary:
Video of convicted double murderer shows him in 2020 deploying a Taser at close range to an Indigenous man’s face, chest and neck

  • Get our

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon, the double murderer who killed Jesse Baird and Luke Davies while he was a serving New South Wales police officer, had been under review by the force for repeatedly using his Taser on a man four years before the killings.
On Wednesday, he was convicted after a 12-person jury found he had murdered both men with his police service weapon on 19 February 2024.

During his 10-week trial, the prosecution alleged Lamarre-Condon had misused his authority as a police officer to obtain CCTV footage of Baird, who he had casually dated; stolen training bullets from the police; and taken a weapon from a police station to use in his crimes.
The NSW police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, has offered his thoughts to the families of Baird and Davies and condemned Lamarre-Condon.

“The actions for which Mr Lamarre-Condon has now been convicted are abhorrent and completely at odds with his oath of office as a police officer which he undertook. His actions are unacceptable to me, the NSW Police Force and to any member of our community,” he said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird (right). Composite: NSW supreme court

blocks.text: “I also wish to acknowledge the professionalism and dedication of those officers who conducted the investigation into the deaths of Mr Baird and Mr Davies.”
But the trial’s revelations have raised questions about how NSW police recruits its officers.

“If police recruitment processes and then police professional standards can let this guy get through all the gates, we need to review our checks and balances,” Dr Justin Ellis, a University of Newcastle criminology lecturer, told Guardian Australia.
“Authority figures are expected to meet higher ethical and behavioural standards, and in this case, the additional responsibility that comes with being a police officer.”
The circumstances surrounding Lamarre-Condon’s recruitment and ongoing employment are being examined by a coronial inquest and a critical incident investigation, NSW police said in a statement.
Terry Goldsworthy, a criminologist at Bond University and former detective, suggested the force revisit Lamarre-Condon’s assessment to see whether any red flags were missed.
He added that Lamarre-Condon’s case is an “extraordinary exception” rather than indicative of systemic issues in the police.

But Ellis believes this type of framing, which narrows focus to individual actors, must be taken into wider consideration of the police processes that “may have enabled the ‘bad apple’ to be in place and to stay in place”.
Separate from the police response to the murders, recruitment processes have been probed as part of a broader independent cultural review, released in June.
It recommended the NSW police force change testing and vetting processes that unintentionally exclude capable candidates, following recent downturns in applicants.

Applicants to the police academy are required to undertake a psychometric test, but former police officer turned criminologist at Macquarie University, Vincent Hurley, said “anyone can bluff a questionnaire”.
He said police should, and may already have, reviewed Lamarre-Condon’s psychometric testing, as well as any complaints by the public or other officers about his behaviour.
Years of staff shortages are placing pressure on recruiting and retaining officers, which can lead to complaints being overlooked, Hurley said.

Four years before the murders and about three years into his policing career, Lamarre-Condon became the subject of an internal police review after video emerged of him repeatedly deploying a Taser on an Indigenous man in the face, chest and neck.
During the June 2020 incident, Lamarre-Condon yells, “If you move, I will Taser you,” before pulling the man to the ground and firing his stun gun.
The man says: “Are you serious? I’m trying to protect my face, I’m not even fighting you.”
An internal review by NSW police cleared Lamarre-Condon of any wrongdoing, finding that he had complied with policy and training guidelines.
after newsletter promotion
‘Haters like to hate’
Police faced intense scrutiny after the murders first occurred in 2024.

blocks.caption: Then NSW police commissioner Karen Webb addressing media in February 2024. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP

blocks.text: Then police commissioner Karen Webb came under fire when she described the killings as a “crime of passion” and responded to criticism by saying: “There will always be haters. Haters like to hate. Isn’t that what Taylor [Swift] says?”
During the trial, it was revealed Baird did not believe he could report Lamarre-Condon’s stalking and controlling behaviour to law enforcement because of his role in the police.

Even if he did report the officer, Hurley said there was a chance police may not have taken him seriously because he did not fit the mould of a “stereotypical” victim of such behaviour – referring to the fact he was not in a heterosexual relationship.
Hurley said Baird and Davies’ deaths were a “wake-up call” for police in how such matters are handled.

The independent NSW MP Alex Greenwich, who helped facilitate a 2024 vigil for Baird and Davies, said after the verdicts: “This tragic and heartbreaking violent crime tells us we need to do everything we can do to increase awareness, reporting, support and access to justice for LGBTQ victims of stalking and violence.”

blocks.caption: A Pride in Protest press conference in Sydney on 27 February 2024. NSW police were asked not to march in the Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras that year, days after Lamarre-Condon was charged. Photograph: Australian Associated Press/Alamy

blocks.text: People in the LGBTQ+ community have long faced discrimination when engaging with police and the justice system, with a 2022 special commission of inquiry into LGBTQ+ hate crimes revealing police reluctance to thoroughly investigate homicides and assaults involving gay men and transgender women.
Ellis, who is part of a NSW police force taskforce established in response to inquiry, said police have an opportunity to renew their engagement strategies with the LGBTQ+ community.
“The more that they’re trusted and people have confidence in them, the more likely [people] are to report to the police.”
In the wake of the murders, NSW police reviewed and implemented changes to the force’s firearms policies and procedures, which have been welcomed by Hurley and Goldsworthy.
At the time of Lamarre-Condon’s arrest, the NSW police force launched its critical incident investigation, which is ongoing and being monitored by the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission.
The investigation will also be reviewed by the police’s professional standards command.
Eventual findings from the ongoing coronial inquest may offer recommendations for the police.

articles.title: VP Sara wants relentless crackdown on illegal drugs
articles.summary: “Dapat relentless talaga yung paghahabol sa ilegal na droga. Maraming problema ang nagsisimula sa iligal na droga… Kaya dapat kinokontrol , sinu-suppress at ginagawang almost zero ng gobyerno ang…

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 10:20pm
Vice President Sara Duterte said that she wanted a relentless campaign against illegal drugs.
According to a "24 Oras" report on Thursday, the vice president had an interview with former Communications undersecretary and pro-Duterte vlogger Mocha Uson, who asked about Oplan Tokhang.
Oplan Tokhang is the campaign of former president Rodrigo Duterte, Sara Duterte’s father. The campaign became synonymous with the bloodY drug war, which saw the deaths of at least 6,000 people.

“Dapat relentless talaga yung paghahabol sa ilegal na droga. Maraming problema ang nagsisimula sa iligal na droga… Kaya dapat kinokontrol , sinu-suppress at ginagawang almost zero ng gobyerno ang iligal na droga,” Sara Duterte said.
(The pursuit of illegal drugs should be relentless. There are a lot of problems that start from illegal drugs… Illegal drugs should be controlled, suppressed and made almost zero by the government.)
The fight against illegal drugs was one of the flagship projects of former president Duterte. However, it was widely criticized by both local and international human rights groups.

Rodrigo Duterte is now detained in The Hague, Netherlands, and is awaiting trial before the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity in relation to the drug war. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Donations to One Nation from two Gina Rinehart associates to be probed by electoral authorities
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Australian Electoral Commission to review $1m in donations to Pauline Hanson-led party from Adam Giles and Ian Plimer

  • Get our

blocks.text: Major donations from close associates of One Nation’s billionaire benefactor, Gina Rinehart, will be reviewed by the Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) amid concerns they were made on behalf of a third party.

The special minister of state, Don Farrell, said on Thursday that information about two $500,000 donations made to the Pauline Hanson-led party could be subject to further regulatory action if they are found not to comply with provisions in the Electoral Act.
In April, Hanson thanked two of Rinehart’s closest associates and senior executives for their “investment” in the party at the same time as she unveiled a private plane gifted to her by Rinehart.

The geologist Ian Plimer, who is an executive with Hancock Energy and known for his climate denialism, and Adam Giles, the head of Hancock Agriculture and former Northern Territory chief minister, each donated $500,000 to One Nation.
At the time, Hanson thanked “two wonderful patriotic Australians” for the combined $1m in contributions.
The money – and the use of the new Cirrus SR22 G7 plane – which can retail for about $2.1m, prompted Labor to accuse One Nation of being “a wholly owned subsidiary of Gina Rinehart”.
A question on notice about the donations from Plimer and Giles asked if the government had “any concerns that these donations were made on behalf of a third party”.
In answer, Farrell said the Electoral Act required relevant disclosures to be made within 2025-26 annual financial disclosure returns to the AEC, due earlier this month.
He said information about donations and in-kind support to political parties, including One Nation, would be published on the AEC’s transparency register on 1 February.
“The AEC will examine disclosures and determine whether further regulatory action is required,” Farrell said.
Guardian Australia has reported extensively on Hanson’s links to Rinehart, including her repeated failures to properly declare free flights on the mining magnate’s private jet.
Hancock Prospecting and One Nation were contacted for comment on Thursday.
The Coalition raised concerns with the federal government about whether Plimer and Giles had made the donations on behalf of a third party, asking if the source of the money would be investigated.
after newsletter promotion
Crossbencher David Pocock also sought more information about the donations, using a parliamentary question on notice to ask if the AEC could investigate their source.

Guardian Australia reported in September that James Ashby, formerly Hanson’s chief of staff and now the party’s national director, drives a new Ford Ranger that was “personally” gifted to One Nation by Giles in April.
Hanson said the vehicle would help the party’s campaign efforts and “provides us the presence we need in the lead up to the next federal election”.
Hanson celebrated the defection of Liberal Leah Blyth to One Nation on Thursday, suggesting the senator would “build on One Nation’s expanding support” in South Australia.

The defection sparked recriminations from within the Coalition, even as Blyth struggled to justify her move to a party she has previously criticised – and as she fumbled key policy positions held by Hanson.
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, called Blyth “a turncoat” while the deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, said her former colleague “wasn’t a big contributor” to the Coalition.

In an interview with the Australian Financial Review on Thursday, Hanson insisted she was not controlled by Rinehart, pointing to her party’s opposition to the Australia-European Union free trade agreement.
Rinehart would benefit from the deal, including provisions to ease tariffs on beef and critical minerals.

articles.title: ‘Disaster’ unfolding as Sydney fire ant outbreak partly blamed on ignored biosecurity recommendations
articles.summary:
Farmers’ federation president says Australia ‘can’t even keep [illicit] cigarettes out of the country … let alone some of these difficult-to-detect pests’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Years-old recommendations by Australia’s biosecurity watchdog have been ignored or not acted on by successive federal governments, increasing the risk of an invasive pest outbreak such as the fire ants discovered in Sydney this week, according to experts.

Environmentalists and biosecurity experts warn the large colony of red imported fire ants are a warning sign that the country’s quarantine system is too slow-moving, underfunded and overly concerned with agriculture.
The nest was found in Auburn and is the second outbreak of the invasive species in Sydney this year after they were discovered at the Enfield intermodal logistics centre on 23 September.
Both sites are industrial areas dealing with imported goods.
The NSW agriculture minister, Tara Moriarty, said on Wednesday that the Auburn outbreak was “different to what has occurred in the past and is seemingly the result of infested imported goods”.
“Our government is boosting our on-ground resources and establishing a taskforce to focus on tracing the supply chains that have led to this occurring,” she said.
But experts say there have been years of warnings about Australia’s biosecurity, often not acted on by the federal government, that might have made a difference in halting the ants’ spread.

The policy director of the Invasive Species Council, Carol Booth, pointed to a 2021 review by the inspector general of biosecurity of the controls for the Khapra beetle, which made recommendations to improve the entire quarantine system.
The South Asian beetle is the second-highest identified national priority plant pest, due to its risks to the grain industry.

At the time, the inspector general made 13 recommendations, including that the department “improve its level of regulatory agility”, “with an expectation of response time frames of days or weeks, not months or years” due to the rapidly-evolving risk of outbreak.
It also criticised the federal government for not acting when the risk of the beetle arriving was first identified in July 2020.

“This delay is an illustration of the department’s continuing regulatory immaturity,” the inspector general found, suggesting either a poorly defined risk assessment process or an overly cavalier attitude to risk.

Four years later, nothing had been done about the recommendation to improve response times. An October 2025 review of the report by the inspector general found that all but one of the recommendations were still open.
Booth said the recommendation was particularly significant because biosecurity risks to Australia were endlessly evolving and increasing, partly due to climate change.
“There are just so many things they should be doing that they’re not, or they weren’t doing well, or they weren’t auditing to ensure that their measures were being actually implemented,” Booth said.
“There’s definitely some things they do well, but others, they just don’t have the resources.”
The Guardian understands the recommendation has since been implemented.

Hamish McIntyre, the president of the National Farmers’ Federation, said farmers “believe we are watching a national biosecurity and human health disaster unfold in front of our eyes around fire ants” due to a failure of the quarantine system.
“We can’t even keep [illicit] cigarettes out of the country through our borders, let alone some of these difficult-to-detect pests.”
He said being an island nation was Australia’s greatest biosecurity advantage.
The federal minister for agriculture, Julie Collins, said the government had delivered over $2bn in additional biosecurity resourcing since 2022.
after newsletter promotion
“This includes more than $296m in the current red imported fire ant eradication program,” she said.

“In the last financial year alone, federal biosecurity officers inspected almost 350,000 commercial sea and air cargoes, preventing tens of thousands of harmful pests, diseases and weeds from entering Australia.”
Tom Kompas, a professor of environmental economics and biosecurity at the University of Melbourne, said it was likely that Sydney’s infestation was broader than currently thought.
“If it does get into metro Sydney, it would be a disaster. It would be an absolute disaster,” he said.
Tax the importer
Australia has a reputation for extraordinarily tough and strict biosecurity controls, but no system can block, inspect or decontaminate every container of every pest.
“We’re going to have incursions of fire ants, among other things,” the Invasive Species Council CEO, Jack Gough, said.
“The key is basically how early in the biosecurity system we’re catching these things, such that then it’s a lot easier to deal with.”
While the Enfield site had been subject to pest inspections, Gough said there had been “clear failings” because its fire ant mitigation process did not match the ant’s biology.
Lures were only placed in some businesses once a year, but ants can move after six months, he said. They were also placed too far apart, further than the 40 or so metres the ants will roam.
He said this was partly due to underfunding and an overreliance on mitigation in the private sector.

Kompas said the biosecurity system was hampered by its approach to risk, with funding against an individual pest allocated according to concern levels. According to him, a better approach would be to allocate funding based on an assessment of cost effectiveness and suggested testing Australian cows for foot-and-mouth disease is probably overfunded.
He said the system placed an overemphasis on mitigating risks to agriculture rather than the environment.
Ultimately, it falls to the taxpayer to pay for eradication, Gough said. Queensland’s fire ant eradication program costs more than $100m a year.

The Invasive Species Council has long called for a new tax on importers to fund the country’s biosecurity system, but Gough said Australia’s obligations under World Trade Organization agreements had prevented its implementation as a flat fee.

articles.title: Nicholas Ty takes oath as new Deputy Ombudsman
articles.summary: Lawyer Nicholas Felix Ty took his oath on Thursday, November 26, 2026, as the new deputy ombudsman for Luzon.

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 9:47pm
Lawyer Nicholas Felix Ty took his oath on Thursday, November 26, 2026, as the new deputy ombudsman for Luzon.

Before his appointment, he served as an undersecretary at the Department of Justice (DOJ), overseeing legal and inter-agency initiatives, including efforts to address human trafficking and transnational crimes.
Upon taking his oath, Ty expressed gratitude to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for giving him the continued opportunity to serve in public office.
In his new role, Ty said one of his priorities is to serve as a loyal soldier to Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla to help fulfill the latter’s goal of eradicating corruption in the country.
“Ang mga priorities natin bilang Deputy Ombudsman ng Luzon ay siyempre tulungan ang kasalukuyang nakaupong Ombudsman si Ombudsman Boying Remulla,” Ty said.
(Our priorities as Deputy Ombudsman for Luzon are, of course, to assist the sitting Ombudsman, Ombudsman Boying Remulla.)
“At ako naman ay magiging isang tapat na sundalo dito kay Ombudsman Remulla upang matuloy talaga ang kaniyang hangad na masugpo ang korapsyon dito sa bansa natin,” he added.
(And for my part, to be a loyal soldier to Ombudsman Remulla so that his goal of stamping out corruption in our country can truly be achieved.)
Ty said he believes the experience and insights he gained during his stint at the DOJ will prove useful in his new position at the Office of the Ombudsman.
He vowed to remain faithful to the Constitution and his sworn duties to hold violators accountable.

“Maging tapat talaga sa Konstitusyon, maging tapat sa mga batas, maging tapat sa mga tungkulin ng isang public servant at talagang maging ehemplo sa ibang mga public servant at siyempre tulungan ang ating Ombudsman para panagutin ang mga taong lumalabag sa kanilang mga obligasyon,” the new deputy ombudsman said.

(To truly be faithful to the Constitution, faithful to the laws, faithful to the duties of a public servant, to truly serve as an example to other public servants, and of course, to help our Ombudsman hold accountable those who violate their obligations.)
Ty graduated from the University of the Philippines College of Law.
He earned his Master of Laws in International Economics and Business Law from Kyushu University in Japan.
He has practiced law for more than 20 years and has also taught as an assistant professor at the UP College of Law. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Muni Network: Newsrooms unite against AI disruption
articles.summary: Facing the threats of AI-induced disruption and declining web traffic, Southeast Asian newsrooms unite through the Muni Network for the future of news

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – As artificial intelligence continues to squeeze traffic and revenue from independent media, the question of what path newsrooms need to take to survive the disruption has been at the forefront of many conversations within the industry.

Some independent newsrooms in the Philippines and other Southeast Asian countries are going a step beyond talking. From November 19 to 22, editors, technology leads, and newsroom strategists from these news groups gathered at the Rappler headquarters to confront the issue and explore approaches to addressing the AI enigma that capitalize on their collective strengths and communities.

Organized and hosted by Rappler, the event, Future of News (FON) Laboratory, aimed to build a collective approach to AI disruption, declining website traffic, and unfair policies by tech platforms, striving to secure, as its name suggests, the future of news.

“Since the launch of AI overview, we have seen a 50% to 70% drop in our organic traffic coming from the search engine,” said Wahyu Dhyatmika, CEO of Indonesia’s Tempo Digital. “We have to find other ways to ensure that we still can reach our audience, can still be impactful, and also build a new business model.”Rappler CEO Maria Ressa stressed the need for a shared solution. “It doesn’t matter if one news group is moving ahead because we cannot fight these forces alone,” she said.

Ressa emphasized the need for newsrooms to find new business models and build audiences together. “That’s the other reason I wrote The Fight Back. The fight back literally is building our communities. It is bottom up with our communities, and then we have to work with our governments,” she explained.

“The November 2026 sessions follow many preliminary meetings and one-on-one sessions where we confronted difficult questions that usually got in the way of collaboration,” said Gemma Mendoza, head of strategic programs at Rappler.

blocks.caption: FORGING ALLIANCE. Editorial leaders and representatives from Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), Mizzima (Myanmar), Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao) pose for a group photo during…

blocks.text: Newsrooms that sent participants to the Future of News Laboratory included Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), and Mizzima (Myanmar), alongside Philippine community newsrooms Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and SunStar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao).

Among matters discussed in preliminary sessions was Meta’s aborted effort to implement a clause in its commercial terms, which treated presence on its platforms as permission for the tech giant to scrape publisher content and use the same as training data for its AI products.

blocks.caption: MUNI-MAXXING. Some representatives from Southeast Asian newsrooms engage in a workshop on how to set up, configure, and maximize MUNI in their workflows. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: “Meta’s recent decision to withdraw the planned website-crawling clause in its updated commercial terms proves that collective pushback works,” said Mendoza, who also leads Rappler’s Future of News initiative.
Representatives of participating newsrooms agreed that they cannot afford to lower their guard.
“They (platforms) steal data, they use data. And the irony is we buy data back from them,” said Redempto Anda, editor-in-chief of Palawan News.

Aryo Widhy Wicaksono from Indonesia’s Katadata also noted that because people now read news straight from social media and AI summaries instead of visiting news websites, fewer brands are buying ads from publishers.
“All the news that we produce, we took effort, we took time, we took a lot of work to do that. And then the AI just took an overview [of] it without really doing anything,” Wicaksono added.

While calling out unfair practices by AI companies, the FON participants also explored ways by which newsrooms can use AI safely to improve and enrich their daily work, as long as human editors stay in control.
At Cambodia’s Kiripost, AI is already helping small teams work faster.
“Recently, our data team, without any coding experience, started a few months ago with vibe coding,” shared Tharum Bun, its co-founder and managing editor.

blocks.caption: THOUGHTS ON AI. Cambodian media company Kiripost managing editor Tharum Bun discusses his newsroom’s unique strengths and the impact of AI in their journalism. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: “Small web tool apps that we have never had before, now we can build in a few months, and we can produce more visual data and stories in a very effective way,” Bun added.
For Mildred Galarpe, editor-in-chief of SunStar Cebu, AI initially felt like a “shining, shimmering tool” that tempted newsrooms to adopt it without enough caution.

blocks.caption: COLLABORATION. SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief Mildred Galarpe suggests community engagement efforts that newsrooms should implement, during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: Galarpe noted, however, that moving too quickly led to early mistakes, such as accidentally swapping the family names of the new and old governors in their coverage due to AI use. That experience taught them that while AI is an effective tool to fast-track work, it is not the editor.

“The human eye should always be there. Nothing should be published without your thumbprint,” Galarpe said.Rappler’s Ressa further stressed that AI cannot replace humans because its models operate on probability instead of facts, meaning what many refer to as “hallucination” is actually just the system working as designed.“You will always need a human in the loop…because news is anchored in facts, but the tech that is ruling our lives, they’re anchored in profit, so it’s corrupted the entire world,” Ressa added.

To turn their stand into action, the participating newsrooms are joining forces through the Muni Network, inspired by the MUNI tab on the Rappler app.The Muni Network will officially launch on December 10, coinciding with Human Rights Day, with plans to expand across the region soon.For Anda, this network is essential for small newsrooms like theirs.

“I look at it as a startup venture, because this is something that is pioneering. You have newsrooms gathering together and figuring out a way to go around this problem of AI using our data [and] how we deal with social media platforms inundating and taking over newsrooms,” Anda added.
By combining their audiences and reach, smaller and independent newsrooms hope to achieve greater impact together, if not match the strength of global tech giants.
“AI doesn’t know boundaries,” Wicaksono said. “If we have a collaboration, we add those small sounds or small voices [to] become one.”

blocks.caption: STATUS CHECK. Some Southeast Asian newsroom representatives put their ideas, capabilities, and ways to respond to AI threats on a whiteboard during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: The federation wants to change how newsrooms work together across Southeast Asia.
Dhyatmika added that publishers won’t stand a chance if they act individually in the era of AI. For him, newsrooms should not see each other as competitors but collaborators.
He emphasized that acting collectively would enable them to get a fairer share of the value created by their products in the digital ecosystem.

Alongside the workshop, the Future of News Laboratory participants also attended Rappler’s Social Good Summit centered on the theme “We, The Humans” — a timely reminder that humans (the journalists in this situation) must remain in control of technology and use its potential to drive meaningful action instead of being driven by it.
Before the November sessions, the group had also issued a joint statement to sound the alarm on the negative effects of AI on journalism, facts, and democracy.

Released last May for World Press Freedom Day, the joint statement highlighted issues such as algorithmic suppression of news, the economic challenges posed by Big Tech monopolies, and the rise of disinformation, which collectively threaten the survival of independent media.

Early collaborators have already launched public chat channels to strengthen local journalism and held community chats around newsroom-initiated investigations. Among those who participated were Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu. Both newsrooms have their branded chat channels embedded on their respective websites.

In September 2025, in time for World News Day, the collaboration also released an experimental video simulating Replica, an “AI-powered journalist.” The video aimed to send a dire warning about what could happen if independent newsrooms die and the only source of news would be AI, ending with a call for citizens to support real journalism. – Rappler.com

articles.title: EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets, but challenges remain
articles.summary: The agreement eyes new export and investment opportunities for Jakarta and Brussels. But can Indonesia turn Europe's growing interest in its markets and critical minerals into sustainable gains at…

image.caption: Economy minister Airlangga Hartarto (2-L) hailed a 'new chapter' in EU-Indonesia tiesImage: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner.

At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people.

The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China.
For Indonesia, it offers opportunities to attract investment, expand exports and strengthen its position in global supply chains.
The agreement will gradually scrap tariffs on more than 98% of product categories, covering almost the entire value of bilateral trade over 15 years.
Indonesia and EU finally seal landmark trade deal
Indonesia's strategic importance to Europe

For the EU, gaining better access to critical raw materials, particularly nickel, and diversifying its supply chains are central to its strategic partnership with Indonesia, said Philip Schleifer, an associate professor of political science at the University of Amsterdam.

"The main strategic interests are opening up a large and growing market for European companies, diversifying and deepening its economic partnerships, reducing strategic dependencies on China, and securing access to critical raw materials," Schleifer told DW.
Indonesia's mineral resources are particularly important for Europe's green and digital transitions. Nickel, for instance, is a key material for batteries and electric vehicles.
The agreement also creates opportunities for European investment in strategic sectors, including electric vehicles, electronics and pharmaceuticals.

But Indonesia has its own industrial ambitions. The government wants to move beyond exporting raw materials by developing domestic processing industries and retaining more value from its natural resources.

"The challenge for the EU is to reconcile its own interest in securing raw material supply with Indonesia's industrial development objectives," said Eline Blot, a senior policy analyst at the Institute for European Environmental Policy (IEEP).
Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US
Export opportunities and challenges for Indonesia
For Jakarta, the agreement offers opportunities to expand exports, attract investment and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

Yose Rizal Damuri, an economist at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said his institution's study estimates Indonesian exports could increase by around 60% in the coming years.
"Not only can Indonesia increase exports to Europe, but it can also become more strongly integrated into the global supply chains of European companies," Yose told DW.
Potential beneficiaries include labor-intensive manufacturing sectors such as textiles, garments, footwear and furniture, alongside other Indonesian commodities and manufactured products.

The agreement could also encourage European investment and create employment opportunities. However, Yose stressed that access to the European market does not automatically translate into higher exports.
He identified three priorities for Indonesia: raising awareness of the agreement among domestic businesses, strengthening production capacity and improving the country's business climate.

"Various trade agreements signed by Indonesia have relatively low utilization rates. The value of exports using these facilities remains limited compared with overall export values," he said, emphasizing the need for better information and outreach to producers.

Syafruddin Karimi, an economist at Andalas University, also highlighted the opportunity to diversify Indonesia's export markets and reduce dependence on major trading partners such as China, the United States and regional Asian economies.
However, he warned that Indonesian producers must improve their compliance with European standards.
"Products must be traceable, including whether their production involves environmental damage or labor practices that undermine human dignity," Karimi said.
He added that smaller businesses would need greater government support to meet requirements concerning raw materials, production processes and workers' rights.
Is Europe still a global power? The brutal free trade debate
Environmental costs of economic integration
The expansion of trade and investment could also increase environmental pressures, particularly in nickel mining, palm oil production and manufacturing.

IEEP analyst Blot warned that increased production without stronger environmental safeguards could worsen pollution, ecosystem degradation and industrial emissions. "Nickel mining and processing can contribute to pollution and ecosystem degradation, while palm oil remains closely associated with deforestation," she said.
The growing importance of Indonesian iron and steel exports also raises concerns about emissions from energy-intensive production.

The EU's Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) presents another challenge for Indonesian producers, particularly small-scale farmers who may lack the resources, technical capacity and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance.
Blot acknowledged that these requirements could create disproportionate costs for smaller producers and potentially favor larger companies.
However, she cautioned against using smallholders' livelihoods as an argument to weaken environmental regulations.
Some Indonesian smallholder organisations, she noted, have supported the EUDR as an opportunity to improve accountability in the palm oil industry.
"Rather than weakening environmental requirements, the priority should be to ensure that smallholders receive adequate financial and technical support to meet them," she said.

Professor Schleifer at the University of Amsterdam also warned that growing global demand for Indonesian natural resources could create environmental and social problems previously associated with commodities such as timber, palm oil and coal.

While Indonesia has considerable bargaining power because of its mineral wealth, the challenge is ensuring that increased demand translates into domestic industrial development rather than simply expanding resource extraction.
How a leading EV supplier covered up toxic pollution
Can Indonesia turn market access into sustainable growth?

The agreement includes a dedicated Trade and Sustainable Development chapter covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, sustainable forest management and labor rights. It also provides mechanisms for cooperation and civil society participation.

However, there is no guarantee these commitments will be implemented. "Experience with other EU trade agreements suggests that there is often a big gap between sustainability commitments on paper and outcomes on the ground," Schleifer said.
Blot similarly called for a time-bound roadmap with measurable objectives, stronger monitoring and meaningful participation from civil society and local communities.

For Indonesia, the challenge also lies in preparing domestic industries to compete. Karimi stressed that the government, both at national and regional levels, must work with businesses to improve production standards, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises.
Yose also emphasized the importance of a predictable business environment, warning that frequent policy changes and regulatory uncertainty could discourage investors.
"Without improvements in the domestic business climate, this will not become a reality. Everything will remain good on paper but will not turn into real momentum for change," he said.
Ultimately, the trade agreement offers Indonesia an opportunity to strengthen its position in international trade and attract investment from Europe.

But whether the agreement delivers broader economic benefits will depend on the country's ability to develop competitive industries, move into higher-value production, and ensure that environmental protection and workers' rights are not overlooked.
DW's Muhammad Athif Aiman contributed to this article.

articles.title: CHR maintains stance vs. abortion except in extreme cases
articles.summary: CHR maintains stance vs abortion except in extreme cases

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 9:32pm

The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) on Thursday stood firm on its pro-life position, saying it opposes abortion except for when a woman's life is at risk, or if she is a rape victim, or there are medical grounds for the procedure.
This was brought up during the Senate plenary deliberations into the proposed P1.285-billion budget of the CHR for fiscal year 2027.
During the session, Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III asked the CHR of its current stand regarding abortion, considering that there have been efforts seeking to decriminalize it.

“The official stand of the Commission on Human Rights is pro-life. They are anti-abortion, except in extreme circumstances, for example, life-threatening, second, victims of rape, and medical reasons,” budget sponsor Senator JV Ejercito answered.
Sotto said he would no longer propound any more questions if the CHR is maintaining its position against abortion.

“Thank you for that because there is an ongoing hearing. I understand that they are trying to revise the Revised Penal Code. So, hearing that from the CHR, I have no more questions and I have no problem with the budget, Mr. President. I fully support the submission,” he said.
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri, meanwhile, also welcomed CHR’s take.
Describing himself as a "Republican" conservative lawmaker, Zubiri said he is "pro-life."

“We appreciate the fact that you came out stating that you will not support legislation to that effect to decriminalize abortion because ayaw po nating mangyari katulad ng Estados Unidos na ano lang, parang pwede kang pumunta ng mall at magpa-abortion [we don’t want to be like the United States where people could just go to a mall and get an abortion],” he said.
“Over my dead body will I allow legislation to that effect, which shall allow decriminalizing of abortion while I’m here in the Senate,” he added.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) earlier maintained that abortion is a crime, but admitted that it was open to proposing exemptions with proposed amendments to the Revised Penal Code (RPC) pending before the House of Representatives.

A DOJ committee reportedly prepared a draft Criminal Code of the Philippines which aims to amend the RPC. A DOJ official also said there were efforts by some progressive lawmakers to decriminalize abortion. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Ex-Cale88 co-owner, BOC official to testify in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada, who is also the Vice President's dentist, is expected to testify on Cale88's organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and…

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte talks to supporters as she prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.
Noel Celis/Reuters

Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada, who is also the Vice President's dentist, is expected to testify on Cale88's organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and financial affairs

MANILA, Philippines – A former co-owner of Cale88 Foods Corporation, who is also Vice President Sara Duterte‘s dentist, is expected to testify before the Senate impeachment court when her trial resumes on December 1.

The defense counsel submitted a manifestation dated November 25 asking the Senate impeachment court to issue subpoenas ad testificandum et duces tecum to Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada and direct her to participate during the proceedings scheduled from December 1 to 4.
Lebosada was also directed to bring certified true copies of the following documents:

items: Registration documents of Cale88 Foods Corporation, including relevant government records;
Documents relating to Cale88’s operations;
Documents relating to the company’s finances and business transactions; and
Other documents relevant to the foregoing.

blocks.text: Cale88, a banana chips production company co-owned by Lebosada and Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, came under scrutiny during the impeachment trial after Anti-Money Laundering Council records showed that it received P776 million in cash inflows despite having only P125,000 in paid-up capital and declaring P208 million in sales.

Lawyer Alex Cabrera, who prepared a forensic financial report on Duterte’s bank and financial records, described Cale88’s business model as “implausible” and likened its operations to a “revolving door,” which he said was indicative of money laundering.
Lebosada is expected to testify on Cale88’s organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and financial affairs.

The defense also sought a subpoena for Agaton Teodoro Uvero, deputy commissioner of the Assessment and Operations Coordinating Group of the Bureau of Customs. Uvero is expected to testify on Cale88’s exportation records under the custody of the BOC.
The impeachment court confirmed the issuance of subpoenas to both witnesses.

“As of this morning, Thursday, November 26, 2026, the Office of the Clerk of Court has completed service of both subpoenas — serving the Office of Bureau of Customs Deputy Commissioner Atty. Agaton Teodoro O. Uvero personally at 9:05 am, and serving Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada in Davao City via electronic mail at 9:54 am pursuant to the Court’s electronic service directive,” said impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol.
The impeachment trial is currently on hold to give way to Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget. Proceedings are scheduled to resume on December 1. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record
articles.summary:
The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid?

Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present…

blocks.text: Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.
It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

blocks.caption: Lana Nusseibeh in March, when she was the UAE’s minister of state. Photograph: Abdelhadi Ramahi/Reuters

blocks.text: Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.
The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.
“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.
The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.
A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

blocks.caption: Fighters who defected from the RSF gathered in western Omdurman, Sudan, earlier this month. Photograph: Marwan Ali/AP

blocks.text: Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”
That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.
Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

articles.title: Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
articles.summary: Officials say the man confessed to travelling at speed and clipping the fuel truck as he was overtaking traffic.

blocks.text: Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.

The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.
Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.
Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.
The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".

"He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."

At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.
Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.

articles.title: So, your personal info was hacked in a breach. Here's how scammers use it against you

image.caption: While it may come as a relief when a breached company says financial information wasn't accessed, cybersecurity experts explain that doesn't mean your bank accounts are safe. (Graeme Roy/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: The hacks just keep coming.

Canadians have been hit with a string of data breaches recently, with companies and organizations such as Bell, Staples Canada's printing website, KPMG, Pattison Food Group and Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children all reporting cybersecurity incidents in the last few months alone.

In many cases, personal — but not financial — information was accessed by unauthorized third parties. Bell and Staples Canada both confirmed no financial information was exposed in their recent breaches.

items: Data breaches are coming fast and furious. Are businesses doing enough to protect your data?

blocks.text: While it may come as a relief to those affected that their credit cards and bank accounts, at least, haven't been compromised, information such as mailing addresses, passwords and phone numbers were.
That's enough to increase the risk of falling victim to identity theft or a financial loss, according to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada.
Bell cyberattack raises fear AI is making data breaches easier

When companies say that no financial data has been stolen, or that the breach was small, people tend to think the breach wasn't that serious, said Ali Dehghantanha, a professor in the school of computer science at the University of Guelph and a Canada Research Chair in Cybersecurity and Threat Intelligence.

But he said criminals can stack and merge the personal information taken from multiple breaches — a piece here from Bell, a piece there from Staples — and use it to try to access your finances, often with the help with AI.
"Once you stack them up, it becomes much easier to scale your attack and targets a much wider and bigger audience," Dehghantanha told CBC News.
"Companies judge each breach alone. But criminals add all of them up. And that's what gives the criminals the upper hand."
How hackers use personal data

While companies at the centre of some of the most recent breaches, such as Bell, said no financial information was compromised, our identity alone can be linked to financial information, said Jeff Horncastle, an outreach officer at the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

"They can potentially have enough information to be able to compromise existing accounts, get into existing accounts or apply for new credit with the information that they've gained," he told CBC News.
"And if they're missing any information, they may be behind a different type of fraud where they're phishing for the information that they're missing."

items: Bell says it's investigating cyberattack that led to potential theft of business customer data
Staples Canada says customer data accessed during 'security incident' on print website

blocks.text: Scammers can use the information they've accessed from breaches to trick victims into handing over their own financial information on scam calls, Dehghantanha said.
Bell's leak, for instance, included the date and amount of customers' last payment, which call centres use to verify their identities.

People walk bast a Bell store in downtown Montreal on May 7, 2025. Bell is one of several Canadian companies who recently warned customers their personal data had been accessed by hackers. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)
If someone has access to a bill you've paid recently, they now have your phone number, and can call you and say your payment for a specific amount on a specific date failed, Dehghantanha said.
If the small pieces of information they repeat to you seem legitimate, they might convince you to give them your card information.
"These bills that have been leaked, have been stolen, are now the gateways," Dehghantanha said.
The scam can also go both ways. Criminals can call companies pretending to be person whose information they now possess, and ask to have their phone number moved to a new SIM card.
So, next time you log into your bank and it texts you an authentication code, the scammer will get it instead, giving them access to your account, Dehghantanha explained.
What to do if your data was breached
Business are required to notify affected customers of a breach.

If you receive a notice about a data breach, contact the organization directly using its official website or phone number, Horncastle said, because sometimes fraudsters will pretend to be a breached company. (Fraudsters have even been impersonating the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre for years).
You need to be suspicious for at least a year, not a week.Ali Dehghantanha

If your information has been exposed, Horncastle says you should change your passwords and contact your financial institution if needed. Some companies will offer credit protection through either Equifax or TransUnion, but he strongly suggests using both.

Try to find out what information was accessed and be cautious for how it may be used, Dehghantanha said. In the recent Staples breach, for example, order summaries and encrypted passwords were accessed by an unauthorized third party.

A customer shops at a Staples Canada store in Richmond Hill, Ont. on Nov. 17, 2026. Staples Canada said there was a 'security incident' on its staplesprint.ca website in early November, which saw a third party get unauthorized access to certain customer data. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

That could mean criminals now have access to your print orders, which might include wedding invitations, or funeral programs, or job applications, making you vulnerable to scams that target newlyweds, grieving families and job-seekers.
It's also important to keep in mind that most personal information doesn't have an expiry date, and criminals can wait a long time after the initial data breach before they attempt to use it.
"You need to be suspicious for at least a year, not a week," Dehghantanha said.
How can people protect their information?

Horncastle said you should use strong, different passwords for each of your accounts, turn on multi-factor authentication, and regularly monitor your bank and credit card statements, and credit reports, for unusual activity.

In addition, he suggests always independently verifying the source of an email or text message, no matter how legitimate it looks. When possible, log into your accounts using official apps and websites — avoid clicking on links through messages.
"Never share your passwords, banking information or verification codes with anyone over the phone, especially when you receive that contact unexpectedly," he said.
Always be careful about any personal information you choose to share online, he added.
"It may be the missing piece of information for the puzzle."

items: 'That was my granddaughter's voice': Senior suspects scammers used AI in Regina, Saskatoon
Her grandson's voice said he was under arrest. This senior was almost scammed with suspected AI voice cloning

blocks.text: Dehghantanha suggests contacting your phone carrier to lock your number from being transferred to a new SIM card, if that's a service they allow, and setting a unique a pin representatives are required to ask before they can make account changes.

And don't just rely on text messages for authentication, since scammers may be able to access those, he added. Enable the call-back option, or combine the text message verification with another method, such as the unique pin, or your fingerprints for touch ID, Dehghantanha said.
Cellphone number transfer highlights potential security risks

Dehghantanha also suggests every family has their own unique code word, because AI has made voice-cloning technology so convincing that people are often tricked into thinking they're getting a call from a loved one in distress — commonly known as a grandparent scam.
"If a conversation is uncommon, just quickly ask, 'What is the code word?'" he said.
Finally, Dehghantanha warns people to never underestimate how quickly and convincingly you may be targeted after a breach.
"An AI intruder moves fast," he said.

articles.title: Flood watch in place on Vancouver Island as king tide impact continues
articles.summary: A flood watch is in place for eastern Vancouver Island as the B.C. coast continues to deal with a series of storms that are combining with unusually high tides on Thursday.

image.caption: A person is seen near a rushing river in the Nanaimo area of Vancouver Island on Wednesday. A flood watch has been maintained for eastern Vancouver Island as king tides combine with a storm to continue to create hazards for coastal B.C. (Claire Palmer/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A flood watch is in place for eastern Vancouver Island as the B.C. coast continues to deal with a series of storms that are combining with unusually high tides on Thursday.
Swath of high streamflow advisories in place for the rest of Vancouver Island and the South Coast

The B.C. River Forecast Centre issued the flood watch on Wednesday, along with a swath of high streamflow advisories for the South Coast and the rest of Vancouver Island, as between 50 and 100 millimetres of rain were predicted to fall on the island.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) said in an orange coastal flooding warning for Metro Vancouver that "moderate to significant flooding" was expected along coastlines and low-lying areas due to storm surge and very high tides.

A number of evacuation alerts were issued by the regional districts of Nanaimo and Comox Valley on Wednesday, adding to previous alerts from the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation and Parksville, with residents told to be ready to leave at a moment's notice.
A warning to stay away from the river, posted by the Regional District of Nanaimo, is seen on Wednesday. (Claire Palmer/CBC)
The B.C. River Forecast Centre said in its flood watch that residents should stay clear of running rivers and never drive across flooded roads.

"Significant storms earlier in the month have contributed to saturated soils and higher flows, increasing the potential for rapid runoff and flow response during this next storm," the Wednesday flood watch reads.

items: How king tides happen, and what that means amid flood warnings in B.C.
Ahousaht declares state of emergency as storm and king tides batter west coast of Vancouver Island

blocks.text: The king tides currently hitting B.C.'s coast — referring to a phenomenon where cosmic alignments can mean dramatic tides which can be about 0.3 to 0.6 metres higher than the average — are expected to end on Thursday.
ECCC said the water levels could elevate by as much as 0.7 metres during high tide on Wednesday and Thursday.
Grouse Grind closed
While the coastal flooding warnings covered nearly the entire B.C. coastline on Wednesday, high winds and rainfall were also an issue for many areas.
B.C. Ferries cancelled a number of evening sailings between Metro Vancouver and Vancouver Island, citing high winds in the Strait of Georgia, on Wednesday.
3 forces are raising the risk of coastal flooding in B.C.

The Metro Vancouver Regional District said that the Grouse Mountain Regional Park in North Vancouver — which houses the popular Grouse Grind trail — would be closed on Thursday due to the heavy rain in the forecast.

"Park staff will assess and determine if trails are safe to reopen once weather conditions allow. Please stay out of the park for your safety, that of park staff, and first responders," the regional district said on Wednesday.

articles.title: Joshua Kimmich critcizes Bayern bosses over Musiala health comments
articles.summary: Joshua Kimmich has slammed Bayern Munich's leadership over comments about Jamal Musiala's health issues. The bosses have questioned whether the player can return to previous form – and is still worth…

image.caption: Joshua Kimmich feels that Musiala's situation should be dealt with behind closed doorsImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bayern Munich's disappointing 2-1 Champions League defeat at Lille on Wednesday night – in which Jamal Musiala came on for the last quarter of an hour – was overshadowed by comments the club's captain made afterwards.

"It must never happen that something like this is played out at a player's expense. Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than the player, but it's not bigger than the person," Kimmich told reporters in the mixed zone.
"That's an absolute no-go and not Bayern-like," he added.
Kimmich was responding to recent comments made by Bayern supervisory board members Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge.

"If he (Musiala) doesn't return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation with his family, with the player, and, above all, with his agency – because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable," Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told Sky on Friday.
Honorary President Uli Hoeness has described the situation as a "dilemma" for the club, while CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen raised the prospect of talks with Musiala's management and family.
Neurological condition

While theGermany player has struggled with a number of injuries over the past couple of seasons, his health came into sharper focus in August, after he collapsed on the pitch in a couple of preseason matches. He subsequently revealed that he had been diagnosed with a neurological condition which causes him to suffer from occasional "absence seizures."
Kimmich added that criticism of a players' performances was legitimate, but that concerns about Musiala's situation should have been dealt with behind closed doors.
"That's something you should sort out internally, around a table, rather than trying to resolve it publicly," he said.
"It's not that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself."
Talks between two sides ongoing

Meanwhile, Bayern bosses met with Musiala's agents on Tuesday, and clarified the timeline of events, dismissing speculation that the player could have concealed the condition when he signed his last contract extension.

Bayern said the two sides agreed that he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after he had signed his contract extension, which makes him one of the club's top earners and is to keep him in Munich until 2030. Discussions between Bayern management and Musiala's representatives are reportedly ongoing.
